speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister): The house may wish to be informed that the second regular session of the conference of the food and agriculture organization will open on Monday the 2nd of September, 1946, in Copenhagen.
The Canadian delegation to the conference .vill be headed by the Minister of Agriculture, vho led the Canadian delegation at the meetings of the food and agriculture organization held at Quebec and Washington. In addition, the delegation will consist of the following:
Doctor G. S. H. Barton, Deputy Minister of Agriculture (alternate chairman of the delegation).
Mr. J. D. Kearney, the Canadian Minister to Norway and Denmark.
Mr. D. Roy Cameron, Dominion Forester.
Doctor E. S. Archibald, Director of Dominion Experimental Farms.
Doctor J. F. Booth, Department of Agriculture.
Doctor L. B. Pett, Department of National Health and Welfare.
Mr. J. B. Rutherford, Dominion Bureau of Statistics.
Doctor A. W. H. Needier, Department of Fisheries.
Mr. A. Gosselin, Department of Agriculture.
Mr. H. H. Hannam, Secretary, Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
Mr. Clive Planta, Secretary-Manager of the Fisheries Council of Canada.
Colonel J. G. Robertson, Canadian Agricultural Commissioner in the United Kingdom.
Mr. Douglas Roe, Commercial Secretary for Canada (timber specialist).
Mr. J. H. Tremblay, Commercial Secretary (Agriculture).
Doctor W. C. Hopper, Department of Agriculture, secretary to the delegation.

The special meeting on urgent food problems held in Washington last May recommended that the director general of the food and agriculture organization undertake certain studies and investigations and submit his findings and proposals to the next conference of the food and agriculture organization. It also recommended that any conclusions of the conference concerning the establishment of new organizations or procedures designed to meet long-term problems in the production, distribution and consumption of food be referred to the united nations. The conference is, accordingly, being held at an early enough date to enable its conclusions to be reported to the next session of the general assembly of the united nations.

PARIS PEACE CONFERENCE-BIG POWERS AND SMALL NATIONS
speechtext:
1.	Who made a distinction between big powers and small nations, and when and for what particular consideration was such distinction made?
2.	'What are, (a) the big powers; (b) the small nations?
Questions

3.	Who leads the small nations at the Paris Peace conference, and in virtue of what authority?
4.	What is the present international status of Canada? Is she, (a) a big power; (b) a middle power, or (c) a small nation, and why?
5.	Was Canada's status changed from that of small nation into that of middle power? If so, when and why?
6.	What is the difference between, (a) a big power and a middle power, and (b) between a middle power and a small nation?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The expressions "big power", "middle power" and "small nation" are not designations recognized in international law. Article 2, paragraph 1, of the charter of the united nations sets forth that "the organization is based on the principle of the sovereign equality of all its members". Article 23, paragraph 1, of the charter states that "the republic of China, France, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and the United States of America shall be permanent members of the security council". In article 27, paragraph 3, it is provided that decisions of the security council in other than procedural matters "shall be made by an affirmative vote of seven members, including the concurring votes of the permanent members". Apart from the naming of certain states as permanent members of the security council-a distinction also made in the covenant of the league of nations-and the requirement that for certain purposes under the charter the concurring votes of the named states are necessary, there is no legal distinction between the position of all the members of the united nations.

speechtext: When the committee rose last evening at six o'clock we had been considering section 1 of this pensions bill, and I was speaking of two special cases which to my mind called for adjustment. speechtext:
As you know, when the house is in committee no member adjourns the debate because there is no debate; it is just discussion. I rose first, but as a matter of courtesy I let the hon. member have the floor so that he would not be deprived of the opportunity of continuing his speech. I could have kept the floor, but life is short and we should adopt a conciliatory mood in discussing this bill.
As I understand the purpose of the Pension Act, it is to give an opportunity to members of the armed forces who have suffered disability to obtain compensation for that disability in order that they may be placed in the same position as that in which they would have been had they not joined the army. It is simply a matter of equalizing things as much as possible. I ask the minister or his assistant or the former minister to correct me in what I am about to say if I make some statement that is wrong. I consider this matter so serious that we should take the utmost care in dealing with it. But first I should like to refer to a report of the Canadian Press which appears in the papers to-day. This is an excellent report, but I spoke quite fast yesterday and one statement has been misunderstood.
Murder case No. 5 which I gave yesterday to the parliamentary assistant to the minister refers to a boy who came from my county. I have in my mind another file which was transcribed in longhand by the parents of a boy whose number was B-621503 and who came from Toronto. He suffered cruel treatment at the hands of the army medical corps in the maritime provinces. This is another murder case. I believe that in each of these cases the parents are entitled to compensation. No matter what compensation they receive it would not compensate for the loss they have suffered.
I sent this to the Department of Veterans Affairs. After these files have been returned to me by the heads of the Department of Veterans Affairs I intend to send them to the Department of National Defence so that there may be sanctions imposed against those who are not doing their duty as medical men.

Pension Act
What is the use of complaining? When we complain of unjust treatment we are replied to by precisely those who are guilty, and naturally we are confounded. They lie like Ananias, but what they say is taken as gospel. All they do is try to save their own skins. Of course there are able men in the army. While I was fighting the cases of men who were suffering from disabilities I received a letter from a gentleman in Toronto who told me that his brother-in-law was one of the army doctors and that he was a reputable physician and surgeon. I sent him a copy of Hansard which contained my remarks, which were based not upon abstractions but upon facts, and asked him if he had anything to say please to tell me and I would be ready to correct anj-thing that was not according to the facts that I might have stated in the house. I never received a reply.
The dean of the faculty of medicine of Laval university in Quebec wrote to me and said that I had been unfair to some men in the army. I admit at once that some of those who were in the Quebec district were fair.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION- REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: On a point of order, I w-ould ask my very dear friend from Temiscouata if he would not permit this pension bill to go through, and take up this grievance, which has to do with something which happened to a man under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence, with that department. As to the matter of the mother of this man getting a pension, I am informed that at any time sihe is in necessitous circumstances or needs a pension she is eligible to get it. The matter is still under consideration from that point of view. I must repeat the plea which I made to the hon. member for Kootenay East, that this legislation be permitted to go forward on its merits and any grievance be brought up when the estimates of the respective departments are under discussion. I can only ask my hon. friend to do that, I have no right to insist on it.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION- REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Surely. I will tell you, sir, that the kind feeling which the hon. member for Rosthern has for my humble self is most warmly reciprocated, and he knows it. But I am not dealing with a particular case, because I shall mention all the facts. Incidentally I mention one case because I want to establish some principles for the guidance of those who will have to interpret the act. The question is not to railroad this matter through but to see that the act is rightly interpreted by those in charge after it is passed by the House of Commons. If I made a sacrifice to come from my beautiful part of the country,
particularly at this time of the year, I mean to do something; I mean to perform a task; I mean to accomplish a duty, and this I shall do to the best of my ability for the sake of all the men who belong to the Canadian army or real Canadians who were in one of the allied armies-and I hope that this measure will not be a disguised form of mass immigration. It may be that because of the delay between the end of the war and the establishment of domicile in Canada all the troublemakers, the Arabs and the Jews of Palestine, will be permitted to come and settle in Canada and get the same treatment as a truly red-blooded Canadian who has been in the armed forces. To this I object very strongly. But not only that, sir; I want the men of the first great war who have not been dealt fairly with until now and the boys who have been in the army in the second great war, to receive fair treatment and better treatment than most of the boys have received up to now.
Sir, you know very well that it was taken for granted by many medical officers that the boys who complained of some unfitness or disability were complaining because they were slackers, because they were afraid to fight, because they were lazy fellows, because they did not want to drill, and so forth. Consequently they were not given the attention they deserved. It was the same thing when as a lad of ten or twelve I was a boarder at a college. We had a doctor, and every time somebody was suffering from some ailment, a common cold or anything of the kind, he was given the same drug, which was inoffensive. It was good for all, because the children in college were young; they were supposed to be well, and there was nothing wrong with them. When they cut their fingers they received the same treatment as they did when they had a cold.

As I said yesterday, I am ready to give the benefit of the doubt to these gentlemen. I am ready to cooperate with them. To my knowledge Brigadier Melville has done very well in some cases, although he is somewhat handicapped by the large burden he has to carry as head of the pension commission. I say to Mr. Woods, the deputy minister, that I am ready to cooperate with him. I consider that his appointment is a progressive step over the maintenance of his predecessor in office.
Pension Act

The pensions question is a big question. If things have to be equalized they have to be equalized in all fairness and in all justice to all. Because Mr. So-and-so has applied for a pension it does not follow that he should get it while the other fellow who is just as worthy of a pension cannot get it. On the other hand, if Mr. So-and-so is not entitled to his pension he should not get it any more than the other fellow who does not deserve it and does not get it. The minister will agree with me in that. It is simple; it is obvious; it is elementary. What I regret is that we have to preach in the house things which are simple, elementary and basic just because of the atmosphere here. When it is impossible to discuss any question on its merits we have, to discuss it from a sentimental point of view. The minister, his assistant, and all my colleagues know full well that I am always ready to help and cooperate with them in promoting the welfare of the men who have been or are still in the army. I will not mention the details of this case, but I will tell you, sir, when a Victoria Cross winner from far distant British Columbia passes over the head of all the legion to send an S.O.S. to the member for Temiscouata, when one of the great heroes of the last war does that, and when the parents of a child who has been murdered by the medical corps, both father and mother, take the trouble to transcribe the file 'by hand and send it to the member for Temiscouata, I feel just as much honoured as if my breast were covered with all the medals of the commander in chief of the allied armies. If those people do that it is because they believe that there is a man who lives far away from them, whom they have never met, who is ready to fight their case against anyone. In this instance I hope that I shall not fight their case against anyone, that I will fight their case with everybody and finally obtain success, and I hope it will not take too long.

speechtext:
I know that, but I appreciate the fact that I have been singled out by these people. They have written to me, although they have never met me. I do not say that in a boastful spirit, but I say it because I have done my very best. Perhaps it is the only reward I shall get, but I appreciate it the more for that. I give credit'to the Minister of Veterans Affairs and to his parliamentary assistant, as I did yesterday. When-

ever I spoke to them they gave me the attention that the cases deserved. That was most appreciated; and it is precisely because I have confidence in them that I again appeal to them to see to it that all wrongs are redressed and that justice is done those who have suffered so much. Here is the file. I told the parliamentary assistant I would not mention the facts, and I have kept my word; but I have enough confidence in them to give them my private files. I have nothing to hide; it is my public duty. Other hon. members are in the same position; I am sure they also have to take up cases which have been sent to them by Canadians whom they have never met, and because that has been their experience I appeal to them to help me in my struggle for these poor men and women who suffered so much anxiety during the war, while their loved ones were in the fighting lines.
That having been said, I have a great sorrow in my heart because of the fact that the young men have been told most dangerous things. They were told that a million jobs were ready for them; that when they came back jobs would be waiting. It was not true. Probably it was said in good faith, and again I give the benefit of the doubt to those who said it; but it is precisely because that statement about a million jobs being available to the young men who were to come from the army after the war was not exact that the Pension Act should be interpreted very liberally with regard to them. What often happens? The boys are told that the disabilities from which they suffer existed before they joined the colours. If that is true, how is it that in most cases they were graded A, as perfectly fit? Later they were told, "Well, it happened before you joined the colours, and you are not entitled to anything." How many times did I have to write the minister just because of the stupidity of those who are the heralds, the champions, of red tape. He helped me to redress these wrongs, but it took a long time; and why should these boys have to suffer in the meantime? The mechanism of the pension department should be on ball-bearings that are well greased, so that action may be taken immediately. Why should a boy wait for months, or for a year or two years, before getting an answer which is in accordance with the facts and which satisfies his mind that he has received justice?
This is the more important at the present time because the boys are being induced to accept false theories; they are given a false picture of public business. It would be a matter of the utmost regret if the boys who fought in the forces for many years, or for any length of time; the boys who joined the

Pension Act
colours, soldiers, airmen, sailors or draftees, lost faith in and respect for our parliamentary institutions. To-day I do not rise only as a member of Liberal faith; I rise as a member * of parliament who wants these and all our institutions to be respected by the young men in order that they may have faith in them; in order that they may realize that when they appeal to parliament, when they appeal to any one of those who occupy high positions in the civil service, they are entitled to fair play and justice, and that they shall not appeal in vain. We have reached a time when the question is not that of maintaining popular confidence in any one of the parties or groups in this country, but of maintaining the faith of the public in our parliamentary institutions, and it is up to us to correct all that is wrong in the mechanism of those institutions. It is most important with regard to the Pension Act and with regard to all the acts concerning those who have been in the armed forces. It is important with regard to every piece of legislation. I remember that during the war I complained many times that we were passing legislation only for taxation; we were passing a lot of it, but principally for that purpose. We are still passing a lot of legislation with regard to taxation, but we also pass a great deal of legislation for other purposes. Yesterday the minister had the grace to indicate to me the amount of expenditure likely to arise out of this legislation. It is a very large amount, but I am not entirely satisfied with his answer, and in due course I will ask him to give the house the total prospective expenditure under each of the measures he has sponsored, so that we may know what is going to be done for the men and what it is going to cost.
There is something else. I was about to speak of this yesterday, but my time was too short. When another government was in power I suggested that all taxes should be earmarked so that a Canadian citizen would know what he pays his taxes for. I wonder if it is not possible to earmark some of the taxes that will go to pay the cost of what is being done for the returned men, so the people will know those taxes are being paid as a tribute to those who served their country well, or to the dependents of those who gave their lives for their country. I may be told that the exchequer is a kind of melting pot, that it is impossible to keep track of the taxation received; but I believe our taxes would be paid by the Canadian people with more satisfaction if they could be earmarked in some way.
In conclusion, sir, I hope the act will be interpreted liberally with regard to real Canadians; those who have been bom in this
country or those born outside this country who made Canada their home long enough before the war to show their sincerity. It is very important. Newcomers who have been in other allied armies should not have the same treatment as Canadians. If we make sacrifices for our own people, we are not ready to make sacrifices for the newcomers who come here to take advantage of the horn of plenty which is supposed to be for the benefit of our own people.
Just a few days ago I met an old gentleman -only relatively old, because his heart is young. He urged me to make an appeal about communism. When I replied to him I was speaking of youth and for youth. I said to him, "Sir, I know your grandson; he is a fine boy. The next time you see him, put to him a question. Ask him if imperialism is the kind of theory that appeals to him. He will surely tell you that this is the policy that has been so dear to the hearts of the former generation, but that those boys have not been impressed by it at all. They were coming here as Canadians at heart, ready to do something for this country, and to make it greater than ever. Ask him to choose between communism and patriotism."
Well, communism is not the first choice; patriotism is the first choice. But how is it that we have to reeducate the Canadian people about what was taken for granted by the generation which preceded us? All hon. members have been at school or at college. Were they ever taught patriotism? I was taught in the family. Of course those of the family are dearest to the hearts of the parents, dearer than friends would be. Friends are dearer than strangers. But those who live within the bounds of the home country should have bonds and ties in common because their interests are common. They should have the same ideals. The boys should understand that when something is done for them it is a preferential treatment that is not given only to sailors, soldiers, and airmen. It is a preferential treatment that is given to Canadian sailors, soldiers, and airmen. They must have first choice. The state must do all it possibly can, in a reasonable way, to help them out and to make them understand that their mission is not to cross the border and try to find a livelihood in the United States, where food is now scarce. They will have a better life in Canada than they would have in the United States, and that must be told to them. They must be told, because they will wear the burden of debt which we have increased to such an extent. They must have confidence in their country-in this country. And they will have it only as patriotism is
Pension Act

preached to them. Then, if they have the same principles and the same feelings as we were taught, they will think of Canada first and will never believe in the theory of communism, which is the negation of the rights of the individual.
When I left that gentleman he said, "Well, that is food for thought. I will ask my grandson about it." I knew what the boy's answer would be, because he was a fine youth, like all the young men who have been in the army. I have faith in him; I have faith in the boys who were in the army, just as I have faith in all the youth of this country. But they will need more courage than ever to surmount the difficulties we have put in their way. We must help them to the utmost, so that they will remain as they are to-day, good Canadian citizens, making life better for the future generation than perhaps we have made it for them.

I must say however, as one who now for thirty years has been living closely with this pension problem, and knows much more about it than the hon. member does, that I never heard such demagogic nonsense in the house in that time as that to which I have just listened. Canning once said:
A statesman of the world alone,
A friend of every country but his own.
There is no country in the world has done so much for her fighting soldiers as has this country of Canada. I resent and I repudiate as strongly as I can the assertions of the hon. member for Temiscouata. Look at your estimates. You are a taxpayer, and a soldier is a taxpayer too. There are S690 million this year in the main estimates, and S175 million in the supplementary estimates, making a total of $S65 million. The total cost of rehabilitation is estimated at SI,500 million, and that for a population of a little over 12 million. And yet we get this demagoguery in the House of Commons of Canada!
The heart of parliament is kind; the pulse of parliament beats true. I have sat on every committee since 1919. I have fought the battles of the returned soldier of Canada, and I am still fighting them-now with authority, previously without authority. And I resent and

repudiate silly, stupid animadversion such as we have listened to from the hon. member for Temiscouata.
This parliament will always be generous; this parliament will always be just to the great cause of those who have suffered so in the cause of freedom, the cause of civilization, the cause of Christianity. I say this silly animadversion should be absolutely discarded by members of parliament.

I will tell the minister what I read in the Monetary Times not long ago in answer to a question which had been put by several returned men regarding conscription. This article, which appeared in the issue for August, 1945, is by L.M.V. of Hamilton, and it states:
I have just returned from four years overseas, fighting for permanent peace. I do not think we should have compulsory military service for Canadians in peace time. I do not want a world war III, as I said yesterday, and I am not going to be bullied by anyone here in this house.

I do not wish to detain the committee for more than five or six minutes, because I am a civilian, though coming from a soldier city. I should like to observe first of all that we shall be here until Thanksgiving day if we keep on discussing bills the way we are doing, and it was for that reason, in order to expedite the business of the house, that I took no part in yesterday's proceedings, on these resolutions, particularly as we have in this party, as in all the parties in this house, soldier representatives who are particularly well qualified to speak on soldier legislation.
This is the most important bill that we have had before us for many years. First of all it defines "department" and it repeals and amends certain pension legislation passed in 1927 and 1928. Then it goes on in the second clause to redefine "hospital allowances", extending pay and allowances or compensation to a large number of people.
I wish to speak on two matters particularly. The first is the definition of "department". In these days the work of many departments is being transferred to other departments, and I was hoping that we would have a department particularly concerned with soldiers' welfare. I think one of the main needs of the soldier is for a home for his wife and family to live in. Before the war in the city of Toronto sixty-seven per cent of our people owned their homes, but during the war many of our Toronto veterans lost their homes. That is why I should like to see the matter of houses for soldiers transferred to the department which has to do with soldiers' welfare. As I said, nothing concerns the soldier more than a roof over his head for himself and wife and children, and the fact that our soldiers have not houses to live in is costing the government a great deal of money in allowances. We have a large number of soldiers in our city. Also many soldiers from all parts of Canada have come to Toronto and are going to stay there. No city has contributed more than Toronto in the way of soldiers' aid.
I wish to compliment the veterans affairs committee on the good work it has done for the soldier. Tho hon. member for Temiscouata has referred to a great many matters



Pension Act
this morning. He seems to have inherited the spirit and mantle of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He also wears the old school tie. There are few on the government benches who now do wear the same old school tie.
I visit 55 York Street, Toronto, once in a while and I am pleased with a great deal of the work that is done there. We have a large number of soldiers in this party, including two Victoria Cross men. The government party and all the other parties in the house have a large number of soldiers in their ranks, and I have been content this session to leave to them the discussion of matters particularly affecting the soldiers, because I have felt that they were doing a real job.
I want to compliment the members of the veterans affairs committee on the work they have done for the soldiers. I should also like to compliment the hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for Nanaimo and all the other soldiers who have participated in the work of that committee.
I should like to see the department expanded along the lines I have suggested, so>
that it would really be a soldiers' welfare department. The soldier goes to the soldiers' welfare in Toronto at 55 York street; he gets his grant and gratuities and goes and) puts the money in the bank. Several banks, such as the Dominion at the corner of Yonge and. North Park, do a big soldier business. I have talked to some of the soldiers and soldiers' wives who go there, and I find that they pay in this money they have; they also borrow money; the wife has been frugal while her. husband was away, and they go down to the lawyer and deposit money for a house and the title to it. Now they cannot get into the home. I had hoped that the health and wek fare department would consider this feature, but it has not done so, and there is no other department doing it. I see in the Toronto papers almost every week letters from veterans and their families complaining about this feature of the work, and I wish the department had considered it. I referred to this on Tuesday last on the third reading of the housing bill.
The second matter is this. I appeared' before the veterans committee about it. As you know, this new bill deals with a number of antecedent matters:	the work of the military commission, Department of Civil Reestablishment, the Department of Pensions and' National Health, and- matters going back as far as the acts of 1927 and 1928. Now I wish to compliment the minister, and I was going to compliment the parliamentary assistant, because he comes from a district which is affected by a branch of this work which has

not been attended to; I refer to the Northwest field force of 1885. No veteran in the present parliament can afford to forget what the three prairie provinces owe to those who took part in military operations in that rebellion. I appeared before the committee on June 11 on behalf of the dependents of those volunteers, to try to clear the matter up. A year ago provision was made in the regulations, section 4, as follows:
In this part, unless the context requires, "veteran" means (a) any former member of the Northwest field force who served in a theatre of actual war in the northwest rebellion.
The proceedings are reported in minute No. 30 of the veterans affairs committee. We owe this regulation, I believe, very largely to the present Minister of Veterans Affairs. After a long series. of arguments in the house and before the committee the allowances were extended to the Northwest field force, but in effect it has given no help at all. A "means test" is applied to these people. A means test is the meanest test I have ever seen; it is well called a "means" test as it bears upon these poor people, widows and children who would get about $40 a month but are deprived of it because they receive some small revenue from an old age pension or some other source of income. I had hoped that this would be a real clean-up bill of soldier grievances. That is what it should be. I was hoping that we would conclude a long chapter of suffering and injustice in connection with this branch of veterans' legislation.
I wish to speak with appreciation of the work of the members of this group on the committee, and what they have done to extend the scope of the benefits, especially the horn, members for Vancouver South, Souris, Royal, N.B., and Vancouver-Burrard.
I should also like to express my appreciation of the fact that in this War we have had better doctors, surgeons and nurses. I know two or three of them who were at the university of Toronto when the war started; they served overseas and are now in Canada again, some of them in practice in our city. We have there some of the best surgeons in Canada. One, a former captain of the varsity rugby team, Doctor M. F. Williams, is a very fine young surgeon, now with one of America's greatest surgeons, Doctor Roscoe Graham. It is remarkable what progress preventive medicine, science, surgery, and medicine generally have made in this war.
As I have said, I was in hopes that this would be a clean-up bill so far as those are concerned who did' not get a pension, men who enlisted and actually were accepted for

Pension Act
service after medical tests before one, two, three, four, five boards, who did not find anything the matter with them on enlistment. I agree that subsequent disability should entitle them to pension, and I am sorry the principle has not been adopted. I had hopes of the parliamentary secretary, who was in the chair when I appeared before the committee in 'the interests of the veterans who served in the 1885 rebellion. Very few of these people got anything. There were a large number of them from Nova Scotia, the old Haligonians and numbers from Hamilton, Toronto and other cities in eastern Canada, and some from Winnipeg, the men of the old 90th Rifles. These men pioneered for the whole of western Canada, and were pioneers of the militia too. Some of them served in the South African war, and their children and grandchildren took part in the two great world wars. Realizing the good work which this department has done, and seeing the plight of these people in my walks around my city, I feel it is a great pity that now a clean-up is being made it does not include them under the first section.
That, is all I have to say, Mr. Chairman. I believe the committee as a whole deserves the thanks of the House of Commons for the zeal and diligence and study they have devoted to this question, which is the supreme question in its sacred significance with which we shall have to deal in this or any other parliament.

I should like to inquire of the parliamentary assistant, not about an individual case, though I desire to illustrate the point I have in mind by mentioning a particular case. I wish to find out what can be done for widows and children of soldiers who were released temporarily to go into mining and who, while engaged in that occupation, were killed in consequence of an explosion. The particular case which was drawn to my attention does not come from my constituency, but this man has written to me stating that he had two sons, and both enlisted, one in the air force and the other in the army. The boy in the air force was killed while serving overseas. The other son was stationed at Halifax for about eighteen months, was married, and had one son. This young soldier was released temporarily by the Department of National Defence to assist in mining when that industry needed help. While he was engaged in this work at Luscar, Alberta, there was an explosion in the mine and he was killed. The father writes and tells me that he not only lost two sons but he has to support the widow of one son and also her 83260-2621
child. Can anything be done to cover such unfortunate cases as the one to which I refer? It appears to me hardly fair for a father to lose two sons and then have to support the widow and her children as well.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION- REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: The answer is that if the man was ordered out as part of his military duty he is covered just the same as if he went on any other military duty. But if he got leave of absence without pay he is not covered for anything that happened to him, because the presumption is that he engaged as an ordinary civilian in the occupation and would have the protection which any other civilian has. Several thousand soldiers were let out on leave of absence without pay in order to engage in farm work and so on. They were doing work which had no more to do with the army than that of a great many civilians who never enlisted in the army at all and who were working alongside of them. If they asked for leave to work on the farm and got leave of absence without pay of course they are not covered. It would depend on the circumstances. If this man was ordered to go there as part of his duty he would be covered ; if he got leave of absence without pay presumably he would be covered in some cases at least by the proper civilian workmen's compensation act.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION- REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: The information I have is that the Department of National Defence directed this young man to go and assist in the mining industry. I hope that the parliamentary assistant will do all he can to see that proper consideration is given to cases of this kind.

speechtext: The proof of government policy is in the way it works out, and there are instances in which this act is not working. I may be referring to a part of the act which is most difficult to administer, but just two days ago my attention was drawn to an instance in which suffering and perhaps harm is being done. This particular young man passed his test A-l. He was sent to England, where he took his inoculations. Following his first inoculation he did not feel very well, but he continued his training. He broke down under intensive training in Great Britain, and suffered from shock. He was sent back to Canada in 1944, and the parents were notified that he would be discharged. He did not arrive home, and the parents finally received word from the department that he was being sent to Ste. Anne de Bellevue for treatment for nervous trouble. In May, 1944, the boy came home, but he was accompanied by an escort. Apparently he was a mild psychopathic case, but since that time he has proved absolutely useless on the farm. He is unable to do any work or to assume any responsibility. Before he enlisted he was a fine, strapping young man who was able to do his work and assume any responsibility, but for two years he has been wholly incapacitated. He lost his father, and the mother and another brother are trying to carry on. In spite of the applications and efforts made by the legion and other people in the area, the only report they can get from the department is, "nervous disorders, preenlistment origin, not aggravated by war service, and not pensionable." How do the officials of the department determine that such a case was of preenlistment origin? This boy passed into the army as A-l, and there is nothing on his record. How do they determine that? Do they question him?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION- REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
I should be very curious to know whether they 'have exhausted all the rights under the Pension Act. There seems to be great misunderstanding about the way these things are dealt with. When the first application is made the pension commission goes over the documents and the ruling is made on the

basis of the documents. When that is done, in some cases people immediately consider that the decision is outrageous because they know all the circumstances. All that needs to be done then is to ask that the case be considered by the commission. Then the family doctor can be called or any other evidence. A hearing is set quite readily. It must be admitted that some people try to create the impression that they can get a pension for somebody when nobody else can. There is then a feeling created that you have to put up a big fight in order to get what is coming to you. I assure the committee that if there is any evidence in connection with any of these cases that does not appear in the documents, it can be submitted to the commission. We are giving in this bill more complete recognition to the independent standing of the pensions advocates branch, the veterans' bureau, so that they may feel freer than ever before to fight for the soldier and see that he gets everything he is entitled to before the commission. I should like to know if the case mentioned by the hon. member for Yorkton has reached a point where vive voce evidence has been taken. That would be most important in a case of the kind. Evidence of the family doctor, if they had one, could be given as to his condition before he went into the army. The medical history is examined into most carefully. Neighbours could be heard, or any evidence at all that would show his condition when he went into the army. Suppose he had some sort of nervous trouble and had served in a theatre of actual war where his trouble was aggravated. He would get entitlement for the disability, unless he was covered by one of the three exceptions: first, unless he wilfully concealed it, which would not be the case here; second, unless it was obvious, which would not be the case here, I take it from what the hon. member has said; and, third, unless it was recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment.
I take it from what the hon. member says that this boy entered the army in good health and therefore he would not come under any one of the three exceptions. Even if he had been somewhat emotionally unstable at that time, if that condition was aggravated during service he would be entitled to full pension for his disability. I can only assume that the case cited by the hon. member has not reached the final stage, and I suggest that he take the matter up with the pension commission.

speechtext:
I shall be _ glad to resulbmit the case. I did not submit it myself ; it was submitted by the legion. I advised them to do that, but the legion has not been able to get anywhere with it. I shall resubmit it and take it up with the department.

It may very well be that the matter has not got to the stage where evidence has been heard from his family doctor, friends, and so on.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION- REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Is it not a fact that often the decision is made here by a specialist who never sees the man?

speechtext: That is what I am trying to do. I am not building these cases out of the air. I have actual evidence of occurrences. I am not going to put any case on the record, but I know of a soldier who was wounded; the ligaments of his leg were tom and he was granted a ten per cent pension. The boy's condition grew worse; he was in constant pain and therefore could do practically no work. At times he was laid up completely; all he could do was to help his father on the farm. The department were asked if they could do something about it, and they asked that he be sent in for another examination. He was sent in for another examination and he came back. After I wrote the minister about it the pension was increased to fifteen per cent, which gives him. about $10 a month. The boy still wanted to get evidence with regard to his actual disability.. As a result of the disability he was in a cramped up condition and seemed to be getting no relief at all. His capacity for work was cut down to nothing. He and his father went to the family doctor. After the examination the father said: "I should like to have a report from you as to the actual disability of my son." The doctor refused to give him a report. He said: "I won't give you a report;-I will send it in to the office in Saskatoon." What is a young man to do when a doctor refuses to give him a report?

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION- REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION

suggest that without exception the department has no knowledge that they are not sympathetic toward the returned soldiers in seeing that they get a square deal. This will be borne out by some figures which I should like to give to the committee. I give them partly because there is a feeling that these cases are not dealt with as expeditiously as some hon. members would like. The amount of work the pension commission has done in the last year has been stupendous. As of June 30. 1946, the disability awards in respect of world war II Were 44,199. That is disability awards alone. The dependent awards were 17.125, or total awards made by this commission in respect to world war II alone of 61.324. That means perusing the files, and all that sort of thing. It is a tremendous amount of work. Then when we brought the insurance principle into effect by order in council it meant reviewing thousands of files to give them the benefit of the act. Over 9,700 files had to be reviewed'. Over nine thousand decisions were rendered in respect of restoration of the insurance principle alone. The total annual liability in respect of world war II is as follows: Disability awards, $13,250,190; dependent awards, $12,158,565. The total pension annual liability now amounts to $25,408,755. That is for world war II. Here are the figures for world war I at the same date: Disability awards, 73.079. with a total annual liability of $26,429,474? dependent awards amounted to 16,894, and the annual liability amounts to $10,560,562.

speechtext: Not now.

speechtext: Personally I can say my own experience with the department has been very pleasant, and I have no complaint whatever with regard to the departmental officials. I should like to ask the minister where the final decision rests. Is it with the board; and what recourse does the family of the victim have? I am thinking of a case which has been thrust upon me for the simple reason that the family cannot afford legal assistance, and the boy in question is completely mentally incompetent; he no longer answers when he is spoken to, and his mental condition is such that he is quite beyond the reach of reason. I am not having any satisfaction in dealing with his case. I have written the department a number of times and received very courteous answers. The local doctor is new, a young man who has come there within the last year or so. He is also very sympathetic, but he did not know this boy at the time of his enlistment. The boy has been out of the army for two or three years. He is a victim of sleeping sickness contracted while in the army. His disability is not the result of military service, yet he contracted this illness while in training, and just on the point of embarkation. I should

Pension Act
like to know where the boy goes from here, because he is mentally incompetent and has no means of support whatever.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION- REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: In the first place, if this disability was incurred during service it probably would be covered by the insurance principle which has been reintroduced in the act in respect of service in Canada, so he may find himself in a very different position now from that in which he would have found himself three months ago before this insurance principle was embodied in the law by order in council. In regard to looking after the claims of soldiers, in the first place the Canadian Legion is ready and willing to take up these cases. In addition, of course, there is the veterans' bureau, an organization of men trained in this work, most of whom do nothing else but present these cases and assist in their preparation. They will assist the boy and his relatives to get evidence, and I suggest that the hon. member direct this boy's relatives to the nearest district pensions advocate of the department. If she has any difficulty finding out where that advocate is located, any person in our department could give her the address. There she will find someone who is paid by the country to press the cases of boys like this.

I should like to say a word in regard to these hospital allowances, and I am glad the minister is in his seat. I want to refer briefly to the hospital set-up, and to express the hope that the good feeling now existing between the Department of Veterans Affairs and the general hospitals throughout Canada may continue. I shall take the local point of view and talk about my own municipality of Kingston. There we had five hospitals: the General hospital, the Hotel Dieu hospital, the mental hospital, the D.V.A. hospital and the military hospital. When mental patients are taken in at the D.V.A. hospital, however, they are sent to the mental hospital. In Ontario we have thirteen mental hospitals, one of which is at Kingston. My point is that the government more or less depends on private or other governmental interests to maintain an institution whose doors are open three hundred and sixty-five days in the year; I refer to the mental hospital. I believe that in each of these thirteen hospitals in this province there is an average of over one thousand mentally ill patients. If D.V.A. find it necessary to use the facilities of that insti-
Pension Act

tution, they are always available; and I understand it has been used by the department ever since the last war. I regret to say that in our mental hospitals there are some boys who have been in those institutions for nearly twenty-five years, and who have received fine treatment all that time. I do not think better care is being given mental patients anywhere in Canada than in the thirteen institutions in Ontario.
Then may I say a word in reference to the general hospitals. The same applies there. In Kingston we have a hospital which will accommodate four hundred patients. For the last twenty-five years a large proportion of the staff of this hospital has 'been returned personnel, and the situation is the same with regard to the medical profession. The point I want to bring out is that recently the military hospital was closed and the staff and patients were moved to Barriefield. In the early days, back in 1940, 1944 and 1942, when it was pretty hard to get anything done. I think the department would have been better advised to extend the facilities of the general hospital and use that institution instead of opening its own hospital. It took us two or three years to get the department to realize that they had a service available at their very door. I am glad to say that within the next few days we expect to be opening a new wing, which will accommodate another 125 patients. When that new wing is opened it will probably accommodate a total of 500 patients. In what I have said I have dealt with the matter from the point, of view not only of Kingston, but also of Canada as a whole. In four or five years the public will have something, built by public money. To-day the general hospitals are chiefly private, those receiving endowments. When a person passes away he may leave something as a bequest to these institutions.
I emphasize as strongly as I can my hope that the good feeling which now prevails between the Department of Veterans Affairs and the general hospitals will continue. I believe under such conditions the general hospitals will be only too willing to cooperate.

I agree with what the minister has said, but I was pointing out that perhaps to-day, and for the next few months, they should have some additional assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If additional advocates are required, they will be obtained immediately.
How are they appointed and paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: By the civil service commission.
Are they employees of the Department of Veterans Affairs?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Sometimes a soldier feels that an advocate who is an employee of the government and paid by the government-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I was a former advocate, and I can assure my hon. friend that

Pension Act

pensions advocates have absolute and complete independence. They are not bound in the slightest degree by any government restriction or policy.
