On section 30-Benefit of doubt.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this clause is the one that amends the benefit of doubt section by adding two words "and presumptions." I should like to get some information as to the significance of the addition of these two words-and in referring to a particular case I hope you will understand, Mr. Chairman, that I am doing it for the purpose of getting information. I admit that I am interested in this case and desire to pursue it further, but my main purpose is to ask one specific question.
The case is No. 420676. I have before me a letter, under date of July 4, 1946, signed by Brigadier C. B. Topp, chief pensions advocate, in which he confirms the fact that this veteran gave gallant service during the first world war, was severely wounded in action, was awarded the Military Medal, and that he has been in receipt of a small pension for many years.
Some years after the first world war this veteran developed a heart condition. This was in addition to the condition already recognized as pensionable. The fact that he had received a gunshot wound in the chest led him to believe that his heart condition might be attributable to the wound he had received while on active service. His claim has been pursued on that basis. As a matter of fact, just about all the machinery there is has been exhausted, and now Brigadier Topp says this in his letter of July 4, 1946:
The district advocate, and we at head office of the veterans bureau, feel that a good case for entitlement was made out.
He is referring to the hearing before the appeal board. He goes on to say:
It must he remembered, however, that it is virtually impossible to establish as a fact in such cases that the disorder did or did not arise during service. I
I emphasize the words used by Brigadier Topp, that it is virtually impossible to decide that the disability did arise from service, and equally it is virtually impossible to decide that it did not arise from service. That seems

to be a pretty fair example of a borderline case in which the veteran himself and the veterans bureau and any of the rest of us who are interested in the case feel that the benefit of the doubt should be exercised.
What I should like to know is this. How can this veteran find out whether the benefit of the doubt clause has been broadened by this amendment so that his case might now be given further consideration? Brigadier Topp said in the concluding paragraph of his letter of July 4:
The only means of reopening the claim is by proof of error or production of substantial new evidence. We are exploring these approaches but I am obliged to state that I doubt whether anything more can be done.
It seems to me that in a case like this it is difficult to establish that there has been any error, or to bring forward any substantial new evidence. But I imagine that many a veteran in circumstances such as these will feel, once he hears that the benefit of the doubt clause has been broadened, that it ..may have been broadened sufficiently now to take care of his case. How, I ask, can this veteran and others in his circumstances find out whether the benefit of the doubt may now be exercised to his advantage?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, not only
is our Pension Act based upon the best principles that prevails in other countries, in that a pension may be awarded for any disablement that arises out of or is due to service, but it provides for a pension for any disablement incurred during service. So far as I know ours is the only country in the world which goes that far. Having laid that principle down, that a pension might be awarded to any person because of a disability incurred during service, it must proved, of course, that it was actually incurred during service; because I do not think it was ever the intention of parliament that we should pay a pension in respect of a disability which the man had when he went into the service and which was not in any way increased during service.
The hon. gentleman says that the chief pensions advocate, who works on behalf of the men, as he should in every way he possibly and properly can, has cited this as a case in which it was very difficult to prove that the disability was incurred during service.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And equally difficult to prove that it was not incurred during service.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
That is apparently the
opinion of Mr. Topp.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That is right.

Pension Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The situation with which we are confronted is this. It has been laid down in our Pension Act by section 5 that:1
. . . The commission shall have full and unrestricted power and authority and exclusive jurisdiction to deal with and adjudicate upon all matters and questions relating to the award, increase, decrease, suspension or cancellation of any pension under this Act and to the recovery oi any overpayment . . .
And so on. It goes on:
(2) In any case in which the commission finds that a pension has been awarded by the commission or by the Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada as a result of an error and not as a result of fraud or misrepresentation or concealment of material facts on the part of the applicant, if such pension has been paid for not less than five years and its cancellation or reduction would, in the opinion of the commission, result in undue hardship to the pensioner, the commission, in its discretion, may ratify the payment already made and may continue payment in whole or in part.
The effect of that is this, and it cannot be emphasized too strongly. Parliament in its wisdom has set up the Canadian pension commission and has endowed it with full power and authority to make rulings in these cases. No other body has authority to interfere with its decisions in these matters. When it makes a decision, it is like a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada. Its decision has even greater authority than a decision of the supreme court, because an appeal can be taken from a decision of the supreme court, but there can be no appeal from a decision of the pension commission except under this section which provides for reconsideration of the case by the commission itself if an error seems to have been made. It comes down to this; is it the thought of parliament that this system is working better than some other system by which are provided appeals for? At one time we did have a system of appeals, and it was found that it worked so much to the detriment of the veterans that with one accord veterans across Canada said, "We do not want this system any longer"; they wanted a system such as we have to-day. Some hon. members seem to think there should be a power in the minister to overrule the commission. Of course no responsible veterans' body wants it left to a minister to have the right to overrule the decision of the commission-an independent board of judges. So it comes back to this: are members of parliament confident that the present board of pension commissioners is enforcing the Pension Act and giving the benefit of the doubt as it should be given under the act which they are sworn to administer?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
They are doing it.
63260-263|

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I think it was established at hearings before our committee that while there might be some difference of opinion about close cases-there are bound to be such -the pension commission had the confidence of every single member of that committee in the matter of their making an intelligent and generous approach to the administration of this act. When my hon. friend says, "They made a decision; it was adverse to the person I am interested in, what do I do now?" the aeswer is that what can be done is all set out in the act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has misunderstood me.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Let me say this, if my hon. friend will be patient for a moment: we are changing this section by adding the words "and presumptions." If there are any cases which are on the borderline the commission will, naturally, if it is brought to their attention, look at this change we are putting into the act; they will bear in mind the intention of parliament in adding it, and assume, I suppose, that we did not do it without some desire to strengthen their powers to lean in favour of the applicant. Some people may say that the words "and presumptions" do not strengthen the act at all; others think it will strengthen the hands of the commission in giving the benefit of the doubt to applicants. I suggest to my hon. friend that he bring the case he mentioned to the attention of the commission when this change becomes law. But, unless it is intended to change the very basis of this act, the Canadian pension commission, while it has the confidence of parliament, must be the body to decide these matters.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I want to thank the parliamentary assistant for the information he gave me in the latter part of his remarks. But in all fairness I must point out that the first part of what he said should not have been directed at me at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I assure the hon. member that it was not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I want to make it clear that I accept the principle that the pension commission should be independent, and that parliament should not seek to override its authority. That is not our purpose in giving examples such as we have given in this chamber. But at the moment we are changing the basis, on which the Canadian pension commission operates. We are, I hope, broadening the significance of the benefit of doubt clause, and I think it is germane to ask what meaning there is in that change; hence my question
Pension Act

as to how a veteran such as the one I mentioned could go about taking advantage of that changed situation. Remember he has been told that he has exhausted all the machinery. I am glad to have now the word of the parliamentary assistant that, despite the fact that he appears to have exhausted all the machinery, he can now, himself, through the pensions advocate, or I can myself, bring his case before the Canadian pension commission and ask them to consider whether a case such as this, which is on the borderline, is not now covered by the power which parliament is giving to the commission to draw on a presumption in favour of the applicant.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the intention of the amendment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The presumption in this case, since there was a clear doubt, should be in favour of the veteran. I will certainly see to it that it is again brought to the attention of the commission.
Will the four thousand Polish soldiers who have been allowed to settle in this country be entitled to the benefits of this act?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I must tell my hon. friend at once that that question has not yet been definitely determined. As soon as it has, I shall be very glad to give the requisite information. In the allied veterans benefits bill, which will be considered by the house, certain provisions have been made which will be explained in detail when that bill is under consideration.

I thank the hon. gentleman. I hope, on the other hand, that those who were responsible for the bombing of the King David hotel in Jerusalem will not be allowed to come to this country to blow up the Chateau Laurier.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is a question entirely outside the jurisdiction of this department, but it is in the jurisdiction of His Majesty's government in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Just to reassure my hon. friend, none of this legislation will affect those who were not domiciled in Canada at the time they went in the armed forces of Canada, its allies, and other members of the commonwealth.
What is the definition of "domicile"? It is pretty hard. There is no definition of "domicile".

I think it would be unfortunate if hon. members were to gain the

impression that this amendment to the benefit of the doubt section of the Pension Act means very much.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Don't take our last hope away from us.

The way in which these two words "and presumptions" came to be added to this section was this. During the discussions in the veterans affairs committee some of us suggested that a presumption should be written into the act to the effect that a man's condition on his admission to the service was in fact his condition at that time, and that if there was any subsequent deterioration during service it would be the responsibility of the state to show that that deterioration was not caused by this service. A presumption of that type was actually passed by the committee unanimously. I read it out in the house yesterday: it was passed on May 31 and is contained in proceedings No. 25 of the special committee. But a week later the Minister of Veterans Affairs told the committee that he could not agree to having that presumption written into the act; that what he would suggest was that we put the two words "and presumptions" at the end of the old benefit of the doubt clause. Government supporters moved an amendment according to our motion to report the bill as it had been approved section by section. That is the reason we now find these words "and presumptions" in the present bill. Obviously they mean practically nothing, because the word "presumption" is not found anywhere else in the Pension Act. This amendment does not tie in with anything; it is just put in as a government suggestion to get away from putting in a proper presumption clause. So there is no point in anyone thinking that the veteran is getting much assistance by the addition of these words. Mind you, if the Minister of Veterans Affairs is kind enough and wise enough to accept the amendment which I offered yesterday, which would follow this benefit of the doubt section and would set out the presumption I had in mind, then the words in the benefit of the doubt section would mean something. They would then refer to the new presumptions section; my suggestion was that there should be a new section, 63-A, which would read:
In respect of an application for entitlement to pension arising out of world war II, there shall be a presumption that the condition of the member of the forces as recorded on his acceptance was in fact his condition at that time and that any subsequent deterioration during service was due to such service; subject to the provisos contained in paragraph (c) of subsection (I) of section 111 of this act.

Pension Act
These provisos are three in number: That the condition was obvious-as for instance if a man had a wooden leg and notwithstanding that was accepted; or that he had wilfully and deliberately concealed his condition; or that he had a condition which had been recorded on a medical examination prior to enlistment. Those are the three provisos to the proposed presumptions clause.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I appreciate the force of the amendment which the hon. member is proposing, but it would not cover the kind of case to which I refer, many examples of which, I am sure, he himself is familiar with, namely, the veteran of world war I whose condition, for which he is now seeking pension, is a post-discharge and not a preenlistment condition. Either we need something more than the hon. member is proposing in his amendment, or we need to be assured that these words "and presumptions" in this clause mean something.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I just say a few words? My good friend the member for Vancouver South and I have debated this issue for two or three years, and we are not in agreement. I honestly think that section 62 of our act gives more of the benefit of the doubt to the veteran than any of these new presumption clauses adopted on the suggestion of one of the British ministers about two years ago. I honestly think that with this amendment, and the generous and sympathetic interpretation of the Canadian pension commission, the veterans will be very well considered. The adoption of the British system would be a definite handicap.

In what way?
Mr. 'MACKENZIE: I believe it is narrower than ours. I may be wrong, but-
No one suggests that we should cut out the benefit of the doubt section.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But my hon. friend last year suggested'-
I never suggested for a moment that the benefit of the doubt section be deleted.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I agree with that, but my hon. friend suggested that we adopt the language of the British system. We had a British officer before the committee the other day, and after listening to him there I say that they are far behind us in regard to the interpretation of the benefit of the doubt clause. We are miles ahead of them.
I have his evidence here, which I will read.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend and I have the same cause at heart, and I think he is impeding the end in view by not accepting the present suggestion.

Reading this clause, I do not think it covers a case I know of where a man was taken into the service as A-l, medically examined and examined later at another depot. He was absolutely all right, A-l, right through for a year and a half, and later was discharged. This man now has sight only in one eye. The reason he has not had a pension is that, as the commission say, his trouble arose in infancy. Evidently the medical examiners when they examined him were in error. I had letters from the employers of this man as to his condition before he joined the service-I may say that he went in of his own free will-and they declare that he could not have done his work if he had had poor eyesight. At one time he was a weaver, weaving at night, and he could not have done that work with poor eyesight; yet the pension board say that according to their medical men his trouble was preenlistment. As I say, that man was taken in' A-l and is now discharged E-5, I believe. He is out on a limb without any chance of getting a pension. The commission say that he can engage a private eye specialist to check up on his case and pay for it himself; but that man, even with this clause, is no further ahead. With the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver South he would come in, and I maintain that he should, because he will go through the rest of his life with sight in one eye only, and in a few years' time he may not have any sight at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I say at once to my hon. friend that this government will never accept, so long as I am a member of it, the principle of fit for service, fit for pension. It is a principle which would be most detrimental to the people of Canada as a whole. We must be fair in these things, and we have been fair and generous. This government has been generous-no, I must not say the government, but this parliament has been generous-and we cannot accept that principle, in fairness to the taxpayers of the people of Canada. I will go on any platform in Canada and say so.

Yesterday, when I made a short statement on behalf of the C.C.F. group here, with reference to the Pension Act, I pointed out that there were some things in respect to which we were not in agreement in the committee and that we would watch the operation of this act, be guided by our experience, and make recommendations at the next
Pension Act

session. This is one of the things I had in mind when I made that statement. Like the member for Vancouver South, I remember quite well the discussions that took place in the committee on this particular question. There was a good deal of debate, and I remember the minister taking the same definite position, he took a moment ago-and as a minister and, a member of the government, it is his right to do so. His contention is that by adding the words "and presumptions" in section 63 of the act, as appears in section 30, it will give all the necessary benefits that the committee wanted in their discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

I do not agree with him, but this is one of the things we will watch. We will watch carefully to see how the cases stated by the member for Winnipeg North Centre and others are affected, and, if this does not operate in their favour we will make our position definite when we find that it is so. I wish to make that position clear without further debate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: May I say a few words for the purpose of the record?-because I am afraid that, by reason of one or two specific cases that have been mentioned, a wrong impression may be created as to the manner in which the commission is handling the work. As at December 31. 1945, 7,810 members of the forces who had served in a theatre of actual war had been discharged and the commissioners ruled their conditions as preenlistment, not aggravated by service and consequently not pensionable. However, it should be brought to the attention of this committee that in 81 per cent of all disability claims by those discharged after service in a theatre of actual war, a favourable decision has been rendered.
When was that 81 per cent announced?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That was at December 31, 1945.
I understood it was 76 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It was 81 per cent at December 31, 1945.
I believe the evidence in the committee was 76 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
That may be a different date. In regard to those discharged after service rendered in Canada, the commission ruled the condition preenlistment not aggravated by service in respect of 54,207. As to the extent of service, I think the comfMr. Bentley.]
mittee should have some information. A substantial number or those who went overseas were returned after a short period of service and discharged for varying reasons: obesity, refractory errors, old age, and other conditions which obviously have no relation whatever to their service.
With regard to those whose service was wholly rendered in Canada-and I should like the committee to get these figures- 12,145 were discharged with less than three months' service, 18,790 with less than six months' service, and 23,340 with less than one year's service, a total of 58,572 who were discharged as medically unfit with service of less than one year.
These are not the same group as are in the 54,207?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No, I am not saying that, but I am saying that 58,572 were discharged with less than one year's service in Canada. We have said to all these people that if any disability arose during that service they get a pension in respect of it. That is just how far we have gone in our pension legislation. When it is considered that of those who saw service in a theatre of actual war. which means service anywhere outside of Canada, 81 per cent who have applied for pension as of December 31, 1945, have been conceded entitlement, the committee will have an indication of how generously the commission has approached this problem. I say that with no idea of giving credit to the government. The commission is operating under the statute, and I say that in fairness only to them. That is the purpose of it, and in justice to them I think every member of the committee would want me to say it.

It must be remembered always that these men were accepted as fit for service. Of this number 7,810 went overseas. They were all accepted for service as fit men. They were trained in Canada and taken overseas. They broke down and were brought back to Canada, discharged as unfit and yet cannot qualify for a pension. These are the actual figures. The same thing applies to the 54,207 who saw service only in Canada. The minister has implied that we are asking for a change in the Pension Act to provide that if a person is fit for service he shall be fit for pension. Nothing is farther from our thoughts.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say that.

I am glad to know that the minister did not mean to go that far. Nothing is farther from our thoughts. All we are asking is that there shall be a presumption

Pension Act
in favour of the man that if he is accepted as fit for service and his health breaks down while he is in the service, it was caused by service. It is merely a presumption which can be rebutted by the state. We believe that that will help at least some of these 80,000 cases, where men have lost their health in the forces of Canada and get no compensation for that deterioration.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is what is being done.

The minister has said that the English system is not as good. Actually I hold in my hand the evidence given by the permanent secretary to the British ministry of pensions, Mr. Parker. He gave evidence on May 9, which can be found in No. 14 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee on veterans affairs. Mr. Parker pointed out first of all that in Great Britain they have the benefit of the doubt section, which is our section 62, and which, by the way, is now numbered 63. The British section reads:
In no case shall there be an onus on any claimant under this our warrant to prove the * fulfilment of the conditions set out in paragraph (1) of this article, and the benefit of any reasonable doubt shall be given to the claimant.
In effect it is the same as our benefit of the doubt section. Mr. Parker explained that provision as follows:
On the second clause of that article dealing with the onus of proof, the position is that that article makes it clear that the onus is on the ministry to negative the claim; and to do that it requires evidence amounting, as the high court expressed it fairly recently, to a real preponderance of probability. That, I gather, is a rather legal form of phrase, but I think probably most of us understand what is in fact in mind.
Then Mr. Parker went on to read the presumption clause, and it is a clause of this type that should be written into the Canadian Pension Act. The particular clause reads as follows:
Where an injury or disease which has led to a member's discharge or death during war service was not noted in a medical report made on that member on the commencement of his war service, a certificate under paragraph (1) of this article shall be given-
That is a certificate of entitlement.
-unless the evidence shows that the conditions set out in that paragraph are not fulfilled.
He explained that in this way. He said:
If a man is accepted for service in a certain medical category, there is a presumption that at the time of his acceptance he was fit for the kind of service demanded of a man in that category, and that in the event of his discharge subsequently on medical grounds due to deterioration in his health there is a presumption that the deterioration was due to service.
Then he went on to show how the high court had interpreted that provision, and said:
They said that the presumption is not a compelling presumption but a provisional one, and that in order to defeat the claim the evidence had to show a real preponderance of probability

That is the state's evidence.
-that the condition was not aggravated by war service. Put in other words, the presumption can be rebutted provided there is good and sufficient evidence to do it.
He was asked what was the reason for the British ministry of pensions adopting this presumption provision, and his answer was as follows:
There was a good deal of discussion in the in the House of Commons in 1943 on the provision in regard to war pensions. At the time the government went into the whole matter and they felt that to some extent the criticism was based on misunderstandings and to some extent the criticism had raised points which were worthy of consideration and modification. As a result of a very full review of the whole subject the government decided that in future the basis of entitlement should be expressed in the way in -which I have read it to you. I think in further explanation of that all I can really say is that the government felt that expressing things as they did represented a fair deal for the man and a fair balance.
If a presumption of this kind were written into our law it might make the job of the Canadian pension commission more difficult, but here is a wrong to be righted. Here are men who have given their health for the country and are getting no compensation. That condition cannot be allowed to continue. If this presumption is written into the law, then it will be the responsibility of the commission to bring forward some proof that that man's loss of health was not due to his service. The navy, the army and the air force accepted these men, examined them most carefully, and in some instances kept them for years; they then got rid of them as unfit. There should be some presumption to protect a man who is in that position.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I shall read from the British changes in war pensions, presented by the ministry of pensions to parliament by command of His Majesty. Section 4 reads:
The existing warrant requires that disablement shall be either directly attributable to or materially aggravated by service.
That is the basis in the British warrant. They have to prove that the disablement was directly attributable to or materially aggravated. by service.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: A basic difference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
We do not require any such thing. We say that all they have to prove is that it arose during service. Naturally they
Pension Act

should have something which carries a man a little farther when the only way in which he can get a pension is to be able to prove that his disability was attributable to service. We do not require any such rule at all. With us it may quite clearly not be due to service, but still the man gets a pension if the disability arises during service. I say, therefore, we do not need this presumption, because under our system the man gets the pension if the disability arose during service. Then my hon. friend goes on to suggest that in some way this presumption is stronger than the one we have. I should like to read from this publication of the British ministry of pensions. They say:
His Majesty's government accepts the view that the fact that a man is accepted for service in the present war in a certain medical category may be taken as presumptive evidence that (a) at the time of acceptance he was fit for the kind of service demanded of a man in that medical category;
Of course our pension commission naturally would presume that also.
We have no such provision.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
No, but they are interpreting the law; and they say if a man was taken into the service to dlrive a truck, they will assume he was able to do that or he would not have been brought in for that purpose. But they will hear other evidence. They go on to say:
(b) in the event of his being subsequently discharged on medical grounds any deterioration in his health which has taken place is due to his service. While the minister of pensions will pay regard to any other evidence

Mark that. There is just a presumption that he was in a certain condition when he went into the service, and that any deterioration is due to his service; but they will pay attention to other evidence, weigh the thing and decide whether or not it is due to service. I leave it to any member of this committee whether he would change our system, under which a man does not have to prove that his disability was due to service at all, but simply that it occurred during service, for the British system, where they have a presumption that it was due to service but the medical people can come along and prove it was not, and then if it was incurred during service the man does not get a pension, as he does in 'Canada. Our rule is just as strong, and I think it is being interpreted by the Canadian pension commission just as generously as the rule in Britain is being interpreted by the ministry of pensions there.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: More so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
In deference to the Canadian pension commission I hesitated to say more so, but I submit we can rely upon them to interpret it just as generously. This is the rule, and it is based upon the fact that it need not be proven that the disability was attributable or due to service. This has application to the question whether the disability occurred during service. We let them all in, whether or not it is due to service, if it arose during service. Then there is this further clause, which reads:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean that it shall not be necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall be entitled to draw and shall draw from all the circumstances of the case-
Which I have just mentioned.
-the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences in favour of the applicant.
I defy any person to look at these two sections and say the British provision is anything like as generous as our provision; and I say it is not fair to our pension law to make that suggestion.
Furthermore I understood the hon. member for Vancouver South to say that young men have given their health in the service of their country and are not getting pensions. That is a sweeping indictment of the pension commission. If a man lost his health through service to the country, under this act he is supposed to get a pension. When the hon. member says these young men who lost their health have been deprived of pensions, let me say that when the hon. member was attending our committee he never suggested that the pension committee was not doing its duty under the law. In other words he is making a sweeping indictment which is not borne out by any facts he brought before the committee.
I do not want to go into all the evidence heard by the committee. My hon. friend is suggesting that a decision was arrived at by the committee at one time, and later, after hearing further evidence, the committee arrived at another decision; and the decisions he has been reading to this house are not those which were reported by the committee, which after all are the decisions of the committee. He has been reading decisions which were reached from time to time during the proceedings before the committee. I know why the hon. member is doing this, and it is known to other hon. members of this house. On that committee were many very busy members of the government, parliamentary assistants, chairmen of other committees and

Pension Act
so on. They were not able to attend the sittings of our committee continuously, but they had a right to their opinions on these matters, and they had a right to vote on them. When my hon. friend tries to suggest that the opinion of the committee was something different from what was reported, he is trying to deprive those people of the right to have their recorded opinions recognized. If we are going to get anywhere, Mr. Chairman, surely we must go according to the recorded opinion of the committee, as finally reported to this house. Any attempt to say that what we reported to this house was not the opinion of the committee I submit is making a nullity of what we tried to do. After all, if we are to sit there and discuss these matters and reach certain decisions, and then have hon. members get up and say:	"Oh, but on
another occasion something different was done; on another occasion some other thing was decided", what in the world is the use of making reports to parliament? If we are to have all these things read from the proceedings of the committee, before we came to a final report, it opens up the possibility of considering all our discussions, and I think the committee will agree that we cannot hope to retrace all the steps that were taken in that committee. So I urge my hon. friend not to represent to the house that the committee decided certain things, without adding that later on they decided to report to the house the relevant section in exactly the form in which the final report was made. This is the report of the committee on veterans affairs, as made to this house.
The government members.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend has no right to say that.
It was the government members of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Even the government members have a right to speak in the committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend suggest that government members have no right to express an opinion in committee? It was the opinion of government members that this provision was just as good as anything suggested by my hon. friend. In that we were borne out by the disinterested advice of the Canadian pension commission, which said that this suggested amendment would not enable them to do a better job for the soldier; and I think this house is entitled to pay some attention to that advice. It was on this, I think, that the government members may have acted, and I believe there was nothing very wrong in their accepting the advice of
people of the standing of the Canadian pension commission.

The parliamentary assistant has gone pretty far. He has almost suggested that I was trying to mislead the house, though I do not suppose he meant that. I know he has a way of showing more heat than light sometimes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: We all have our faults, and I do not pretend to be without them.

We found that out on different occasions in the committee. Here, however, he is overlooking one fact, that in connection with this particular recommendation, when the committee passed the proposed presumption clause it was unanimous. It was not a question of a majority and a minority; they were unanimous.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Where is that stated in the proceedings?

When the government
decided they did not want that-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. member say where that is stated in the proceedings?
At page 752; and other hon. members will substantiate what I have said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Does it say it was
unanimous?

It does not say so, but that was the fact. Now when the parliamentary assistant suggests that it was changed, by government members, mind you, who had not been there at the time the section was considered, he is stretching the point rather far.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Is that not true?

Then he himself expressed an opinion about this presumption. I would refer to page 752 of the proceedings of the committee, where I find the following:
Mr. Tucker:	I may say that as long as it
does not lead to misleading people, as Mr. Quelch has agreed with me in saying that it might, I do not think this will do any particular harm. So far as I can see, there is no harm in carrying it, as long as it is quite clear that it will not mislead anybody. Of course, if it is carried, naturally the pension commission people will study it and see if the section that is referred to is comprehensive enough to really cover it. In other words, they will have a chance to look into it.
He has said that the government is opposing this stand to-day on the advice of the pension commission. On this question the advice should go from the house to the pension commission, rather than the other way round. Here is the fact, that 60,000 men in our forces
Pension Act

have been discharged as unfit, though they were taken in as fit. The parliamentary assistant has made no explanation of how their position is to be improved. He is not suggesting for a minute that these men can get a pension or any compensation now. They cannot, under the law as it stands to-day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Is the hon. member arguing that where a disabling condition was neither due to service nor incurred through service, and when a man has come out in just as good condition as when he went in, he should still get pension?
That is not the case at all. Nobody is trying to argue that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is the finding of the commission.

We argue that where a man comes out in unfit condition but went in in fit condition there should be a presumption that such deterioration in his condition was caused by his service. It is true that the state can overcome that presumption by bringing in other evidence. Nobody is asking to make it open and shut, or that a man must get a pension if he is discharged. All we are asking is that there should be a presumption in his favour, that the state, having taken him in as being in fit condition, then having used him for whatever length of time he was in the forces, and having discharged him as unfit, must show that that loss of health was not due to his service. As the parliamentary assistant himself said in the committee proceedings, he could see no harm in that presumption.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is being done.
I cannot understand why the minister and his parliamentary assistant are so firm in their refusal to have a presumption of this type written into the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We have it now.
They keep saying, "We have it now"; but the proof that we do not have it now lies in the fact that 60,000 men can get no compensation.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Proof we have it is that we have the most generous system in the whole world.
Oh, that is old talk.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
To place the facts on the record, the commission said there were 64,207 not granted entitlement after service in Canada only because the preenlistment condition was not aggravated by service. In other words those 54,207 did not get pensions because they

suffered from a preenlistment condition which was not aggravated through service. Those men were in just as good shape when they came out as when they went in.
That is ridiculous.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That was the decision of the commission in those cases.
It was not, at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it was. It was based upon that-the preenlistment condition was not aggravated.
That is like the case brought up by the hon. member for Yorkton.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is their decision. If the hon. member says that decision is wrong, then all he is saying is that the pension commission is not enforcing the law.
I am saying the law is not right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The law says that you give a pension if a man is suffering from disability due to service or incurred during service. The pension commission have to enforce that law, and they have found that when a man came out in just as good shape as when he went in they have no right to give him a pension. That applied to the 54,207 men.
How on earth does the parliamentary assistant make the statement that these 54,207 who applied for pension because of disabilities are just as fit when they come out as when they went in?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is the finding of the commission; that is why they did not get pensions.
Why were they let in?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Oh, that is another matter. That is the "fit for service, fit for pension" principle, which my hon. friend said he would not favour. Then he asks how they got in, and says that if they got in they are therefore entitled to pension.
I did not say that at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the logical conclusion from your argument.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
That is what is meant by your argument, there is no doubt about it. These decisions were arrived at with this benefit of the doubt right in the act. And if you say that thousands of the 54,207 who were ruled not entitled to pension because they had a preenlistment condition which was not

Pension Act
aggravated, are suffering from service, you are impeaching in a sweeping way the work of the commission.
We say the law is not right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That was not borne out by the evidence before the committee.

I have no intention of debating this question over again. However I would lay emphasis on one point, and that is that it was the opinion of the committee, as represented by members who sat through the committee hearings consistently from beginning to end, who listened to the evidence of the pension commission, the legion and other bodies, that paragraph (c) of section 11 (1) had not operated satisfactorily, and that the benefit of the doubt provision was not working satisfactorily. It was as a consequence of evidence heard, and through experience, that certain amendments to the act were moved. The presumption provision was inserted, and the words "wilfully concealed" were taken out of paragraph (c). Then when the government decided they were not satisfied with those amendments they brought in the rest of their members in order to outvote us. The point is that those members brought in by the government had not listened to the evidence of the commissioners or of the legion. They were merely voting the way they were asked to vote by the government. Therefore the hon. member for Vancouver South was sound in his statement that the real desire of the committee was to pass the amendments as put in the first place.

This is one place where
every man should speak for himself. I shall try not to do more than that. I doubt if any member of the committee attended more meetings than I did. I am glad the committee of the whole has had this opportunity to debate the subject, because some of us went through 1,600 pages of it-discussion very similar to what we have had to-day.
When this suggestion was first made by the hon. member for Vancouver South, who, when he keeps his temper, is always plausible, I wras one who at the time could see no difficulty in it. As he was careful to point out last night, I was the person who at a later meeting moved that the paragraph be changed to its present form. I have no apology to make for the fact that I made that motion in committee, reversing my former position. In my experience I have found that on numerous occasions I have had to change my mind, and perhaps even then sometimes I have been wrong. However after mature
consideration most of us can bring better judgment to a question. So far as I am concerned, I have heard the evidence, and as a result of further information and representations made by members of the pension commission-particularly the chairman-I became convinced, as I am still convinced-just as I am prepared to give the hon. member for Vancouver South credit for being convinced of his position-that I should change my mind on it. To suggest that I simply changed my vote because other members were brought in who had not been there before is unfair. The committee, in the fifty-two meetings it held, had perfect knowledge in advance of any suggested amendment from those who were not government members of the committee. There were always benches filled from end to end-and quite properly-and when an amendment was produced by the opposition, once it was either accepted or defeated the chairs were then emptied1 until the next amendment came along. There was no monopoly of absenteeism on the part of the government party in the committee.
This whole debate sounds as if we were sitting in a session two years from now, instead of to-day. I am not a professional veteran, and I carry no torch for the minister or his parliamentary assistant, who are able to look after themselves. But I was one who listened and agreed, listened more and then disagreed; and I am still in the position I was when I suggested that this clause be put in its present form.

I listened carefully to the meticulous and often repeated statements of the parliamentary assistant as to the way in which this provision is working out.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs stated a few moments ago, that it was definitely not a part of Liberal policy to treat veterans on the basis of "fit for service fit for pension". Leaving aside cases often in dispute with respect to the way in which the injury or disablement occurred during service, about which I think most of us have received many letters, may I refer to the preenlistment situation.
This government did during the course of the war take the stand that we were going to have a volunteer army, and it was a matter of considerable pride overseas and elsewhere that ours was not a conscript army. Of course- I know that our boys were not shanghaied into enlisting in the old pirate sense or anything of the kind, but it is debatable whether the enlistments were on a one-hundred per cent purely volunteer basis.
Pension Act

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I remind the hon. member that we are discussing clause 30, dealing with the benefit of the doubt. I would ask him to confine his remarks to that section.

That is the very point on which I wish to elaborate, Mr. Chairman. The government has an onus in the matter of giving the benefit of the doubt which goes back to the time when the veteran was a civilian and was first accepted into the forces. In order to make a good record of recruits ments-and I was a recruiting officer too, as many other members were-I think it is beyond all doubt that the examination of-volunteers as they came into the forces was not as thorough as the examination that is made when the men are applying for pension. I think all will agree on that. When a man came into the service the medical inspection was straight routine. The questions put to the men were often mumbled and the answers noted in such a way that the recruit would be given a clean bill of health provided that nothing organically wrong was obvious. Whether you were a medical man or not you could have inspected and passed many of these recruits. So undoubtedly in our anxiety to appear a one hundred per cent volunteer force, we accepted recruits who perhaps had physical disabilities which, while not obvious and of a kind which in civilian life might have lain dormant for years, came to the surface after a few weeks' hard drilling.
Just the other day many members of the house must have seen parading around- our buildings a man of the type to which I refer, bearing a placard. He was accepted for enlistment in London, Ontario, -according to the documents on his person, on January 17, 1941, and was discharged on April 9 of the same year, after only a few months' service. One might say that that man should never have -been accepted for Canada's volunteer army. But what are the facts? His documents show that he reenlisted on May 18, 1941 and was discharged fourteen months afterwards, on July 23, 1942. He was struck off strength as unable to meet the -required physical requirements. He was a volunteer. He did not leave Canada. He was, in -my non-medical opinion, of the neuro-tic type. I do not want to say that I am a medical expert, but I have no doubt that this man can not meet -the physical requirements, at the present time at least. Someone advised- him, or perhaps he got the idea himself, that he should get a pension. He applied for one -and was turned down by the commission. Possibly his case was one of enlistment under false colours; I am not -prepared to say. I have written to get the documents. All I know about his condi-
tion is what appeared on the documents on his person. I feel that the government has an Obligation to this man because in its anxiety to make a good volunteer record it accepted him -as being in category A-l and fit for service. After enlistment he deteriorated rapidly, as many of them did, and in three or four months he was discharged. Here was a man who was accepted so that our record of volunteer enlistments might be maintained-at least that is the purpose I see back of this enlisting and reenlisting. Therefore the government must assume an obligation for the physical deterioration- of such men, and it is the duty of this House of Commons to make a recommendation to the -pension commission that they take that into consideration-.
I might cite the case of a man in my battery who to my personal knowledge was injured. Fo-r -a year and a half I fought his case, along with other members of the house, before he got a 30 per cent pension for his disability. The machinery is not quite as well oiled and smoothly running as the hon. member for Rosthern would- lead us to believe, and there are other hon. members who know th-at. For that reason I am not in favour of the wording of this section.
Section agreed -to.

Mr. Chairman-, before we deal with section 31 I move:
That the bill be amended by adding as section 30A thereof the following:
The said Act is further amended by adding thereto the following section:
63A. In respect of an application for entitlement to pension, arising out of world war II there shall be a presumption that the condition of the member of the forces as recorded on his acceptance was in fact his condition at that time and that any subsequent deterioration during service was due to such service; subject to the provisos contained in paragraph (e) of subsection (1) of section 11 of this act.
I have already made my position perfectly clear, and I will say nothing further at this time in support of this amendment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: If this amendment means anything at all, and I understand the hon. gentleman contends that it does, it means a possible increase in the charge on the public purse, not necessarily and inevitably, but conceivably; therefore, Mr. Chairman, I submit that it is out of order because it has not received the approval of His Excellency.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I suppose one could argue the other way, that if it does not mean anything in the opinion of the parliamentary assistant, it is perfectly in order. However, this amend-

Pension Act
ment would insert just the same type of section as the benefit of the doubt section, which is not a section involving the expenditure of public funds, but is in the nature of a direction to the pension commission that in considering applications they shall bear in mind this presumption. That is as far as the amendment goes. It is not a matter involving the expenditure of funds at all, and I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that it is perfectly in order.

On the point of order, I should like to emphasize the fact that both the minister and the parliamentary assistant have insisted that this will not bring about any change, any improvement, and if that is true it cannot mean any increase of expenditure. On the other hand, a number of us feel that if it does nothing else it will at least give a certain amount of moral support to the pension commission to exercise a wider latitude in handling these cases.

I did not have the privilege of sitting in at any meetings of the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs, and for my own information I should like to have a clarification of what the minister has said. I brought to the attention of the veterans affairs committee a year ago the situation of a veteran of the two great wars, a case which, I understand, had been fought by the Canadian Legion to get a pension for this particular man. The man went into the last war in category A and came out in category E, and not until recently have we been able, with the help of another hon. member, to get any sort of pension for this veteran. Unless some changes have been made in the act whereby disability incurred during service, such as reduces a man from A to E category, entitles him to a pension, I for one am entirely against this legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just to put it as brieflly as possible, the Pension Act provides that if a disability is due to service it is pensionable; if it arises during service it is pensionable; if there is an aggravation of a condition which a man had when he went into the service, and he has had service in a theatre of actual war, and the disability was not obvious, wilfully concealed, or recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment, he not only gets pension for the disability in respect of the aggravation but he gets it in respect of the entire disability. Of course that does not apply in respect of service in Canada only. If he did not serve in a theatre of actual war he gets the pension in respect of the disability, or the aggravation of the disability, as the case may be, to the extent that there is an aggravation. That is putting it, I think, as simply as I can.
Now, in interpreting whether the disability arose during service or was due to service, we have the section which is in dispute to-day. The way it was worded before was:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean that it shall not be necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall be entitled to draw and shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences in favour of the applicant.
That made the language as explicit, pep-baps, as the English language could make it, that if there was any doubt whether this disability was incurred during service or was due to service, or the aggravation was incurred during service or was due to service, the applicant was to get the benefit of the doubt. I really do not see how it could have been made much plainer; but in deference to the committee and in accordance with what the hon. member for Vancouver South-
That is not what we asked for.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
-in order to make it doubly plain we added the words "and presumptions":
all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.
If an enlisted man was to drive a truck there would be a presumption that he was able to drive a truck.
Why did you not put if in the bill, then?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It is in there already. The only thing I can draw from the hon. member's suggestion is this: we say to-day that according to the best opinion of the Canadian pension board, every man who suffered a disability which was due to service or incurred during service or was aggravated during service is getting a pension in respect of the disability. Some hon. members may say, "I know of a case where I do not think that has happened".
There is one right here.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, the hon. member for Kootenay East has a case which he feels is very strong. I happen to be a lawyer; I have been on one side or the other in various cases, and I have had decisions of the appeal court of our province, and I am just as strongly convinced to-day that they were wrong as I was at the time I fought the case. But the decision of that appeal court had to be accepted by me as correct.
Pension Act

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The hon. member is not casting any reflection, is he?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
If you ask the commission to adjudicate on a close case you are going to have differences of opinion. That is inevitable; you cannot avoid it. And in order to be sure that the pension commission knew the will of parliament that they should give every benefit of the doubt to the man we put in "and presumptions" in addition to "inferences". As I said before, this is a change in the law, and I would expect that in these doubtful cases the Canadian pension commission would feel that parliament was emphasizing this point, and would review these cases in the light of the change in the act to see if their decisions were in line with that change.
My hon. friend is saying that he thinks some people are not getting a pension who should have it under the act as it stands to-day. If that is so, if he is moving an amendment which will grant a pension to somebody who did not incur disability during service, or where-

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, the parliamentary assistant is now trying to make a second argument on the point of order; he is completely out of order himself, and I suggest that you give your ruling.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I was just going to conclude the argument.
He is just trying to make a second argument on the point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Well, I do not wish to press it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Rosthern has answered the question of the hon. member for Assiniboia, and he should not renew or add to his argument on the point of order.
I will give my ruling on the point of order. The question has been raised whether or not the amendment would involve an expenditure of money. I have listened to the arguments since the committee assembled this afternoon; and it has been represented that 60,000 members of the armed forces have been discharged as unfit, although taken in as fit. It has further been represented to the committee that 54,207 have been discharged whose present condition was not aggravated through service.
Those are part of the 60,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Obviously the purpose of the amendment is to bring in a large ciass of former members of the armed forces, some

of whom would under the amendment be entitled to pension, and that would involve an expenditure of money. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: With regard to section 30, may I ask the parliamentary assistant to clear up what I thought was a bit of confusion he created a moment ago. Earlier this afternoon he and the minister both said that the purpose of the addition of the words "and presumptions" was to make a change and to broaden the meaning of the section; but a moment ago he introduced another idea, namely, that the purpose is simply to make doubly clear the meaning already there. speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Our understanding of the present section 62, now 63, is that, inter-pretalively, it is the most generous section in regard to the benefit of the doubt, but the committee felt that this addition should be made, and possibly it might broaden the section. But it will never widen the sympathetic and generous interpretation of the Canadian pension commission, because they are going as far as they can now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is, however, the clear intention that the addition of these two words is to make possible the review of some cases formerly denied.

speechtext: Yes.

I can give my hon. friend the assurance that there will be no

subtopic: VETERANS UNEMPLOYABLE THROUGH DISABILITY- WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE BOARD

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved the second reading of bill No. 331, respecting allowances for war veterans and dependents.

subtopic: VETERANS UNEMPLOYABLE THROUGH DISABILITY- WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE BOARD
speechtext:
There are a few words which I wish to say respecting the War Veterans Allowance Act. This is an act under which allowances are paid to veterans of the first great war, of the preceding wars, and now of course of this war, who have reached the age of sixty, or, in the case of a female, the age of fifty-five, or, third, who in the opinion of the war veterans allowance board are permanently unemployable because of physical or mental disability or who are incapable of or unlikely to become capable of maintaining themselves because of economic handicaps combined with mental or physical inability.
The act has been in force since 1930 and has done a great deal of good for veterans of the first war who have reached an advanced age or who because of war service have become incapable of earning their living.
The present bill not only makes some slight changes in the procedure under the former act but incorporates in its provisions the dual service pension order which was enacted by order in council during the war and which enables the allowance to be granted to certain veterans, who served in both wars, I and II, and who thus have given a considerable period of their life to the armed forces of their country.
On the motion for second reading I shall refer briefly to the outstanding omission from the bill, the omission from the provisions, both of the original part and of the dual service part, of veterans whom we all know as imperials, that is, Canadians who served in the armed forces of His Majesty other than Canadian armed forces in the first great war. Many of these soldiers came to Canada immediately following the war, settled in Canada and became Canadians. The migration
continued until about 1930, when it was considerably dried up because of the depression. But there are in Canada a very large number of imperial veterans who are Canadian citizens and who are deprived of the benefit of the act simply because they did not happen to be living in Canada at the time they enlisted in the armed forces in 1914 or in any of the subsequent years. According to an estimate of the board, the actual number who would be affected were they brought under the act would be 4,639.
I simply wish to point out one or two things in this regard, and I do not wish to labour the question, because the cause of the imperial veterans has been fought and brought before this government for many years. Many of these imperial veterans have been Canadians now for twenty-six years-Canadians in every sense, for a whole generation,-and most of them for more than fifteen years. They have been taxpayers for that length of time. Some of them were soldiers of the first war, and many of them soldiers of both wars. They are the fathers of Canadian servicemen who served in Canada's armed forces, the navy, the army, and the air force in the second war. They have been Canadian producers for a generation. They have been contributing to Canada's wealth, strength and prosperity for all that time. Recently, they have become Canadians by law under the Canadian Citizenship Act. Every hon. member welcomed that act and thought that it represented a new advance. Only a few short weeks since the passage with great eclat of that act we find that Canadians, all of them for sixteen years and many of them for twenty-six years, are not to be considered Canadians when it comes to benefits under veterans' legislation. They are not considered Canadians although in the case of the dual service pension they have actually served in Canada's armed forces in the second great war. All of these men served in a common cause in an actual theatre of war in the forces of His Majesty, and yet in Canada they are deprived of the benefit of these allowances, although other Canadians who served in the Canadian forces of His Majesty are given these benefits, and rightly so, because their services have been as great and because of their present need.
The reasons given by the minister for refusing to admit the imperial veterans when the matter was raised in the committee and was voted upon were two. He said that our veterans' legislation was based upon a great principle; that people coming within its scope must have been domiciled and resident in Canada before they entered the armed forces.

The second reason, was that our first duty lay to Canadians. By that I take it he meant people who were Canadians before they started to serve.

I did not want to speak as long as I have spoken. All I can say is that I do not see eye to eye with the minister in any way on this point. If you want a high principle upon which to found benefits for Canadians who have served His Majesty, then you have it in the service which was given to His Majesty in a common cause. You could not have a higher principle than that.
Let me show the house how this domicile and residence principle as the only principle upon which to found this legislation leads the government into strange inconsistencies. I hold in my hand bill 328, respecting veterans of the forces allied with Canada. This bill goes on the principle that if you are domiciled and resident here, no matter what your citizenship may be, no matter what your business in the country may be, you can get Canadian benefits. I find that an alien domiciled, resident and earning his living in Canada before the war can get benefits in so far as they exceed benefits of his own country, not if he served in the forces of His Majesty, but if he served in the forces of any one of the allied nations in the second war.

That is what I said. I am showing how this great principle which the minister adheres to leads him into strange errors. A soldier of His Majesty and a Canadian citizen for twenty-six years cannot get the war veterans' allowance because he was not domiciled and resident in Canada when he

War Veterans Allowance
enlisted. But an American who joined the forces of his own country, not when we went to war but when the United States went to war; who never served His Majesty but who now returns to Canada; who has not taken and does not intend to take out Canadian citizenship papers, can get the benefits of our legislation while the imperial soldier cannot.
I might go farther in connection with this matter of aliens who benefit under our laws and refer to the principle I have enunciated, that there was service to His Majesty by Canadians in a common cause. Here, however, we have no service to His Majesty, no Canadian citizenship, and it was not even realized by these people who will be benefited that there was a common cause at all until after their own country joined the fight against Germany. Until that time there was not even a recognition of any common cause by these people. I am not arguing the question of bringing these aliens within the provisions of the law; that was all gone over in the committee. From those proceedings, however, it is quite clear that when the government introduced bill No. 328 they were aware of the point I am now raising and they deliberately put it aside, admitting these non-Canadians, while not admitting Canadians who, to my way of thinking, are very much more entitled to the benefit of veterans legislation.
I want to conclude by pointing out how much stronger, if possible, the case I am making is for the admission of imperials to the benefits of the dual service pensions order which is now brought into this act. At the present time a Canadian who was domiciled in Canada and who served in His Majesty's Canadian forces in both world wars comes within the provisions of that order. In addition, a person who was domiciled in Canada and who served during world war I as an imperial, and who became a member of His Majesty's Canadian forces during world war II comes within the provisions of the dual service pensions order. So that we have excluded from the provisions of that order those imperials who had not migrated to Canada before the end of the last war, but who may have been here for twenty-six years, are now Canadians, and who, for the past five or six years, have served in Canada's armed forces. Surely they would have been brought within the provisions of the dual service order if it had not been apparent to the minister that to bring them into that class would necessitate bringing them into the first class as well, and as a result he has excluded them from both.
I shall say no more; I did not want to speak this long, because this case has been argued many times previously. There may
have been some justification before the last war for not bringing in these people, some of whom would not have been in Canada for more than nine or ten years before 1939. In the committee I moved that all those imperials who had been resident in Canada on and since September 1, 1930, should be brought within the provisions of this important legislation, but my motion was negatived. That is a suggestion I want to make to the minister even at this late date. I say to him, with ali the emphasis at my command, that if he does not bring in these Canadian citizens- these men who have given such great service to His Majesty-it will be a shame which will long blot the history of veterans legislation in this country.
