I wish to speak briefly in reference to one phase of this bill, and I imagine the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) is well aware of the phase to which I shall direct my remarks. As he knows, one of the first struggles in which I
War Veterans Allowance

joined when. I came to this parliament was on behalf of the widows of veterans of the first great war. I am glad to see that our good friend the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) has come into the chamber. Everyone will recall the part he played in this struggle, and no doubt he will have something to say to-day as well. One of the requests made for the past three years by those speaking on behalf of veterans' widows was that the special allowance which has been voted from year to year, and the provisions that have been made by order in council, should be given permanent effect by statute. That has been done in the bill now before the house, and I refer particularly to part II. For that action those concerned will be deeply grateful, but I feel that I must express their disappointment that this is all that has been done. These women, whose representatives are well known to many hon. members, were earnestly hoping that as a result of their appearance before the special committee on veterans affairs, and as a result of the consideration given this matter by that committee, there would be other changes and that some of their other requests would be implemented.
The matter, of course, which is of greatest concern to them has to do with the amount of the allowance, which is still fixed at $365 a year for a widow without child or children, and $730 for a widow with children. I realize that when one expresses disappointment that the amount is not larger, that involves a reference to the amount paid to veterans themselves under another section of the bill. My hope was that both amounts might have been increased. For the moment I speak only with reference to the widows, because I desire particularly to draw attention to their situation.
Speaking particularly of the older women who are widows of veterans of the last war, I insist that it is not good enough to ask them to live on a maximum of $30.41 a month. I know all the arguments offered one way and another, including that which states that one cannot ask that a great deal be done for these women until sufficient has been done for other classes. I have never been impressed by that argument. It seems to me it only strengthens the case for implementing at an early date other measures of social security that are long overdue.
The simple fact is that by this legislation we are asking these widows of men who served in the last war to be satisfied with $30.41 a month. The matter was placed before the committee by the women themselves, and the minister is well aware of their request for

an amount of $40 a month. If it were in order I would move such an amendment, but I realize that in doing so I would not be in order. I hope, however, that the government will not regard this bill as the last word on the subject, but that we might soon have an increase in this amount from $365 to at least $480 a year.
These women have made the further request that in the drawing of this measure they be included for hospitalization, and have expressed their disappointment that such a provision has not been made.
Another angle of the matter which affects many of these women is closely related to the observations of the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. Merritlt) concerning the section dealing with a theatre of actual war. As the minister knows, the husbands of many of these widows, although volunteers in the last war, saw service only in England. Upon the death of the husband, without a pension or any other means it is just as difficult for a widow in 'this class to get along as it would be for those widows whose husbands saw service on the continent of Europe. Here again I express disappointment and urge upon the government that further consideration be given the matter, with the thought that even this year, certainly not later than next, the basis for these payments might be enlarged.
The discussion to which we have just listened respecting imperial veterans has its counterpart in widows in Canada of imperial veterans xvho have been able to leave ne other provision for those widows. Their plight, too, deserves consideration.
There are other matters about which I could speak, such as the application of the means test, but they are more in the nature of details, and I shall not discuss them until we reach sections 7 and 8 of the bill in committee. At this moment, however, when we are discussing the principle of the bill I would express pleasure that we have now moved from -the order in council stage to the stage of definite 'egislation on behalf of these women, but would express keen disappointment that that is the only change proposed by the bill before us.
This group of women is not a large one. They feel, and I share their view, that the fact they are not large makes it difficult for them to receive consideration. Their battle began several years before I came to the house, although I knew of their efforts. The sort of thing they had to do to obtain recognition was pitiful. At long last, three years ago, they were given recognition through an order in council permitting an allowance

beginning at $20 a month. I am thinking now particularly of the widows of veterans who served in the last war, but the day will come when these provisions will apply to the widows of those who served in the second war. These groups of widows are small, but their battle is not yet over and I say their rights should have more complete recognition than they have received thus far.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the War Veterans Allowance Act is a good piece of legislation. It has been well administered in the past and, having some knowledge of the confines of the act, I believe the interpretation has been liberal.
We are now making certain amendments to the old act which should make it possible to deal with veterans more adequately in the future than we have done in the past. Had we removed the means test from the Old Age Pensions Act, I have no doubt it would have been possible to have removed it from this one. However, that was not done.
I believe the allowance for a veteran's income is liberal. He is allowed to have an interest in a home up to $4,000, cash in the bank up to $1,500 and an income of $250 plus $125 casual earnings, without any deduction. One criticism I would make is that the government might very well have included the $250 of income with the $125 of casual earnings so that the veteran could have received $375 of income, without any deduction being made. This would involve only a small amount of money, and would save a great deal of confusion in dealing with those two different types of income.
There is no doubt that in the past this act has been a godsend to many veterans, and I have no doubt it will continue to be so in the future, and will help those who are in bad financial circumstances.
Perhaps I might say a word or two respecting imperials. I should like to see war veterans allowances given not only to imperials but to the nationals of all those countries which fought with us in the last war. On the other hand, I believe the matter must be dealt with on a reciprocal basis until, as the minister has said, such time as we can get the war veterans allowances for all Canadians who served both in England and in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is not often a member on the opposite side of the house considers it his duty to say a kindly word to a minister. I am happy on this occasion to do so. In the seventeen years I have been a member, and have known the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), I have always found him
to be a fighter for the rights of veterans. Perhaps he has not always got what he wanted; perhaps he has not always given what the opposition asked, but I believe his heart was always in the right place. One such illustration is found in the case mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
I might say, in passing, that in attending committee meetings at various hours of the day we have been worked almost off our feet. My delay in coming to the house this afternoon was occasioned by my attendance before the committee on Indian affairs where, I believe, I am doing good work.
From the very beginning the Minister of Veterans Affairs has favoured giving consideration to the widows of those veterans who were wounded, returned home and made recovery, but who did not receive pensions sufficient to enable the government, on their passing, to grant pensions to their widows. The minister took hold of the matter right away. I found him from the very beginning strong for giving relief by way of pension to the widows of soldiers who died without sufficient pension to warrant their widows receiving pension. While I have not read the bill, I heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre say that they are to receive $1 a day, or $365 a year. I am not going to say that that is too much or too little, but I am going to thank the minister on my own personal behalf for his work in that regard, for I, too, from the very beginning have strongly advocated that the widows of these soldiers be taken care of. I am glad to know that, while the minister has done that in the last year or two by regulation or order in council, it is now made statutory. That is a fine step in the right direction.
I heard the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) speak of the veterans of the Northwest rebellion, and I am glad to see that they are included in this bill. I do not know at the moment just what they are to receive, but the fact that they are mentioned in the bill is an evidence that the minister is carrying out his promise to make statutory what heretofore was done more or less by regulation. Again I want to thank him for that. When a veteran of the Northwest rebellion makes application for pension I think considerable latitude should be allowed by those who are to determine whether he is to receive a pension or not. They are all old now. because 1885 was sixty-one years ago and they cannot have long to live. Whatever pension they are to be entitled to will be of material help to them and will be greatly welcomed by them. It will be some recogni-

tion of the part they played in that scrap in the northwest which never should have taken place. It was the result of hotheads-

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to delay the house for more than a moment; but I am brought closely in touch with a large number of the imperial soldiers, and I should like to say just one word, a word of pleading more than a word of claim or right, for those men who
FMr. MacNicol.]
served with the imperial forces in the first great war, and then came out to Canada and enlisted with the Canadian forces during this last war. They served mostly in Canada in the veterans guard in the last war on such duties as guarding vulnerable points. These men all getting up in years and are finding it extremely hard, after having served in two wars, to become reestablished' in civilian life at the age of fifty or more. I hope that generosity will be shown to these men. The dual pension, at one time known as the bumt-out pension, was designed, I believe, in recognition of the fact that men who had served in a war aged! prematurely, and men who have served in two wars age prematurely. No matter where these men were serving, in Canada or in a theatre of war, when they are reaching middle age they have suffered more than the young man who actually went over and saw all his service perhaps in England or elsewhere. So that I should like to make a special plea for the imperial veteran who served with the imperial forces in the first great war, then came to Canada and has lived in Canada for twenty-five years or more, and who served in Canada during this war and is now finding it difficult to become reestablished in civilian life. He is denied certain benefits. If he could receive benefits under this act I believe that in the long run it would not cost this country much more money, because he will have to be looked after since he is handicapped in fitting into the civil life of Canada now.
I should like to underline the remarks which were made in connection with the non-pensionable widows. These people had hoped that they would see an increase in their pension perhaps up to forty dollars a month. They also find it difficult to make both ends meet on the pension which the government now allows them.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved the second reading of bill No. 336, to amend the Veterans Land Act, 1942.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext:
I should like to offer a few observations on this phase of the new Veterans Charter, bill No. 336.
The Veterans Land Act, as most hon. members realize, came into being in 1942 with the object of settling veterans, who were qualified, on farms. It was divided into two sections, one for the full-time farmer and one for the part-time farmer, or what is now recognized as the occupier of a small holding, which means a house on a half-acre of land. I thought at the time that was a splendid idea, and it is, but we have run into some difficulties on account of the administration. To be fair to the administrative officers, their task has been pretty difficult, with the present housing crisis, in administering the small holdings and in starting a great number of applicants upon land at the present time. Moreover, things have changed greatly in value since 1942; and with a ceiling of $6,000 to settle a veteran on an area of land and provide a house, barn, granaries, live stock and equipment, it is almost impossible to realize this project in any good district to-day. On the other hand,
Veterans' Land Act

the same ceiling applies in the case of a house and a half acre of land. Everybody knows that building values have skyrocketed. It is impossible now to build the type of house which was intended for a sum of not more than $6,000. I notice in the paper that in Victoria such a house is now costing $7,636, without carrying charges estimated at $1,100 odd, spread over twenty-five years, and in that particular case the veteran, his wife and family agreed that they could not undertake that obligation. Things are going to be difficult in that respect for this administration and for parliament in the near future.
As to the matter of full-time settlement on the land, I want to raise one objection. I wish to be fair to the director. Under order in council P.C. 10472, certain adjustments were made in 1942, I believe, in relation to the old soldier settlers, and since then many have obtained clear title to the land. It may be said in fairness to the director that he has taken all the safeguards possible to protect the new veterans in the purchase of farms to-day, but in some cases the decision of his office works rather unfairly to the new veteran. Let me give one example which will illustrate a good many cases. I have in mind a young veteran who wished to purchase an area of land adjoining his father's farm in one of the best agricultural districts in Manitoba. He qualified as a good settler, made a cash payment, was given his receipts and was told to go ahead with his spring operations. But the administrative officers felt that, because the property was originally owned by a soldier settler of the first great war and this adjustment had been made under the order in council to which I have referred, the purchase could not be effected for this young settler. That is the grievance I have.
I sympathize with the practical difficulties with which the director has to cope, but I still think this is unfair to the new veteran, when one considers that this farm is one of the best obtainable, adjoining land owned by this young man's relatives, where he could borrow necessary equipment and so on. I suggest that everything possible should be done to assist young veterans to make a success of their settlement on the land at the present time, and I hope the administration will relax their regulations a bit in this regard.
Probably no member of the veterans committee has pointed out more consistently than I have done the necessity for taking safeguards to see that there is successful settlement of veterans on the land, but I suggest that in this particular case there has been too much red tape. I repeat, I sympathize with the director and his administrative 
officers; but where land is so desirable, notwithstanding the fact that adjustments were made with the old settler, it is only fair that everything possible should 'be done to see that a new veteran is settled under the circumstances I have mentioned. This case that I have brought forward is typical of a good many others, and I hope that something can be done to meet this criticism.
There is another criticism I made, not only in our committee but elsewhere, and that has to do with the question of war assets. I am aware that I cannot go very far in the discussion of that question under this bill, but I have been keen in advocating that priorities be granted veteran settlers. I would urge upon the government the importance of this, even though I may be somewhat out of order in doing so at the moment. I sincerely trust that something will be done to assist these settlers in obtaining priorities. After the discussion we had yesterday morning in this house, there is further evidence that much of that equipment could be made available first of all to the veterans who are settling in Canada.
So far I have been rather critical-

AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext:
I have just a few words to say and I hope I shall not get into quite as noisy an argument as I did yesterday with the parliamentary assistant and the minister. I can assure them it is not my intention to do so.
I believe that the present bill is a great improvement on the old Soldier Settlement Act which we had after the last war, and there is no reason why it should not be. At that time we were starting something new in this country and we had no experience either of the administration of such an act or in the building up of the necessary organization. It was to be expected, therefore, that we should make some mistakes.
In drafting this bill in 1942, I believe, the government and the committee took into consideration many of those mistakes and tried to draft a bill which would at least, as far as possible, remedy some of the defects. But in doing that we find that probably we created certain other difficulties and made certain other mistakes. Perhaps one of the greatest mistakes in the old Soldier Settlement Act was the fact that it was started in a period of inflation and that there was no write-off in the debt, so that the soldier started with a debt which it was impossible for him to pay under the circumstances which developed later.
In this new bill we decided, in the first place, to see that the soldier had a fair equity in his land. Later, we found, through the increase in the price of land, that, in order to obtain land, we had to reduce that equity,
Veterans' Land Act
and in my opinion we probably reduced the equity just a little too much at the present time.
In 1941 I made certain suggestions-other hon. members did the same-to the effect that the government should have taken over certain types of land and held them for the veterans at the close of the war-certain lands such as C.P.R., C.N.R., Hudson's Bay and mortgage company lands. That land would have been available to the soldier at a reasonable price, the price which obtained at that time. That was not done and, as a result, much of the land to-day is being sold to our veterans, under the Veterans Land Act, at a considerable increase over the 1941 price.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext: Does my hon. friend recall that when he was on the committee in 1942 the advice of all practical farmers was to go very slow with the acquisition of land?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext:
Yes, with the acquisition of improved land. But at the time I did suggest that a lot of this unimproved land should have been secured, if possible, at prices which obtained at that time, or reserved at these prices for later development by the soldier when he returned. This has resulted in the administration having great difficulty in obtaining land for settlement at prices which they believe to be reasonable. That is one of the greatest difficulties for the returned man who has to buy good land in a reasonably sure crop district at prices which the board can afford to pay. The administration are setting prices at approximately the 1941 or 1942 prices of farm land in Canada. If the soldier wishes to obtain that land he must put up the difference between the price that is being asked to-day and the 1941 or 1942 prices. That is going on. in a great many places. The result is that only those returned men who have relatives who can advance or give them money to pay the difference are the ones who are able to obtain land at the present time. It is restricting the numbers who can be settled under the act. I am one of those who were in favour of seeing, that high prices were not paid for land on which these soldiers were to be settled; nevertheless I think conditions have changed in Canada. Our whole price structure is on a higher level. Just the other day the government announced that we were to have a stabilized price for wheat over at least the next four years. That price does justify some increase in the value of land in western Canada. The board would be well advised not to stick too strictly to their present policy of paying not more than the 1941 or 1942 prices. In good crop districts the
Veterans' Land Act

value of this land has advanced to a certain extent and the board should take that into consideration.
There is no doubt that the restricting feature of this bill is the availability of good agricultural land in Canada. There is nothing very much that this government can do about the matter. There is only so much land here. A certain amount of it is under provincial control.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext: Would my hon. friend not commend what we have done by way of agreements with provincial governments with regard to provincial land?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext: Yes; I am coming to that. Most of our natural resources are under the control of the provincial governments. I believe that the dominion government is making a real effort to come to some agreement with the provinces with respect to land. Nearly all the provinces are prepared to cooperate. Some have already signed agreements.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext: Four.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext: Yes; and I believe others will sign in the near future. There is one point with respect to these agreements which I should like to bring out. Under the old Soldier Settlement Act we found that a great number of our returned men were sent into districts where they were thirty or forty miles from the railroad. They were settled on new land which in many places was hard to clear. While they were settled in groups, yet we found that within two or three years many of them became discouraged and pulled out, which left those who remained, in scattered settlements where it was impossible to give them the amenities of life, the roads, schools and other things which are necessary and which we should have in Canada to-day. Most of the provincial governments are trying to overcome that. Some of them have devised different schemes of doing so. They are opening up one large tract in Al'be-rta. They have contracted with a United States firm to clear so many thousand acres of land which will be made available to soldiers. I expect that other provinces will have other agreements. I know it is the intention in Saskatchewan to try to avoid) some of the errors of the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext:
I must say that
Alberta has been the most cooperative of all the provinces.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext:
I am glad to hear that. I knew it would be one of the western provinces which would be in that class. Probably the reason why the minister did not include

Saskatchewan is that he and they do not agree on the methods by which veterans should be settled on provincial land. We believe in that province that, in trying to avoid the pitfalls of the past, we should see that these settlers are placed in groups where we can give them the roads, schools, medical attention and other services to which we believe they are entitled1. That province believes that the principle of cooperative farms should be tried- out there. I am sorry that the government have not seen fit, when they were amending the act, to include an amendment which would have permitted funds granted by the dominion government to be used for cooperative purposes, not only in the buying of land but in the buying of fishing equipment and equipment for any other work which the various settlers wish to undertake in a cooperative way. There should have been an amendment which would have permitted that.
In Saskatchewan we feel that that would have been the best method, or one of the methods which should have been used in placing settlers 'there. Probably we shall be able to work out some satisfactory agreement even under the regulations in the act as it stands at present. Under sympathetic cooperation it is still not impossible to do something along these lines, and I hope that the government will give sympathetic consideration to proposals there. I can assure them that it is the desire, of the government of Saskatchewan to cooperate in every respect, and, along with the dominion government, to assume responsibility with regard to any losses which might occur when settlers are placed in this way. I would1 suggest that the government continue to give sympathetic consideration to the suggestions which are coming from that province.
I should also like to comment on the amendment which we now have before us. I believe that it is a good amendment. There is no doubt in my mind that it will assist greatly in settlement in the better districts in western Canada. There are areas where, at present prices, it is difficult to obtain an economic unit of land.
iMr. ROSS (Souris): The hon. member is referring to leases.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext:
Yes. It is hard to obtain an economic unit under 'the old act where they have to buy. Under the new amendment they will be able to lease an economic unit and obtain assistance in securing equipment to work it. Later, when they have built up a little capital of their own, they will be able to get further assistance in the purchase either of the rented farm or of a new unit on which

Veterans Land Act
they can carry on. So that I commend the government on the amendment 'being made in this act.
The matter of small holdings has been discussed. I believe that when the bill was introduced originally, in 1942, it was expected that the small holdings would be more or less agricultural undertakings; that certain operations would be carried on there in connection with the production of perhaps, honey, the raising of poultry, the planting of fruit trees, and so on. On account of housing situation, however, this part of the act is becoming more and more a housing scheme to-day. I do not agree with that. I admit that under present circumstances this may be necessary, but I have always felt that housing should be dealt with by another department and the small holdings scheme carried out according to the original intention. It was designed to give at least a partial living to people who might be able to obtain other part-time employment, in factories or elsewhere, not only in the larger cities but in the smaller towns as well, and I think would have served a good purpose in this regard. It still can be made use of in that way, but up to the present it has been concentrated principally around the larger cities and used as a housing scheme.
I hope and believe it is the intention of the government to get away from this system as soon as possible and spread the small holdings in the vicinity of the smaller towns. I feel there is a place for this scheme in all parts of the western provinces. There is no doubt in my mind but that very few towns of more than one thousand population in western Canada could very well afford to have from five to ten of these small holdings in the vicinity; and I hope that as soon as present shortages of building materials are overcome the scheme will be extended and these small holdings established adjacent to the smaller centres in western Canada, at least, because I know, from observation covering many years, there has been a natural growth of these small holdings around our towns, operated by people who obtain parttime employment in the towns and carry on these small operations. So I hope that within the next few years the government will make that part of the act work much better than it is working at the present time.
There are other matters with which I shall deal when the particular sections are reached, but once more I want to urge that the government give sympathetic consideration to amending the act to provide for the cooperative use of the money available under it. The government will have to assume the responsibility for not including that provision in the 63260-264
bill. They will have to assume the responsibility if in certain provinces they do not find it possible to settle as many returned men as they would like, because of this restriction which arises from the fact that no provision is made for the cooperative use of this money.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am thoroughly in accord with the amendments proposed in the bill, which I think will help bring about the settlement of more men on the land. I say that chiefly because the price of land has gone up in the last few years, and, as a result, many boys are being forced to rent farms. This measure provides for loans and grants to them.
I supported the Veterans' Land Act when it was introduced in 1942, but at that time I pointed to a number of difficulties under which the veterans would labour. Unfortunately those difficulties have increased as a result of increases in the price of land and equipment, together with the great difficulty of obtaining equipment at this time. I pointed out then that it would be quite difficult for a boy with limited resources to go into fulltime farming under this act unless he could get the help of his parents. Of course, where a boy's parents live in the vicinity they have machinery which will be available to the boy, but not many are in that happy position. Today officials under the Veterans' Land Act are turning down many boys purely on the ground that their financial resources are not sufficient to make it possible for them to start off with any chance of success. Many of those turned down are boys who have lived on farms all their lives, and with good records in the army. They are being turned down purely because their financial resources are not sufficient to ensure them a good chance of success. I am not criticizing the officials for this. When we discussed the Veterans' Land Act in this house we were critical of the officials of the old soldier settlement board for settling boys who did not have a real chance to make a go of it. As a result, the officials are being careful to see that the boys settled now will be likely to succeed.
Having that in mind, when we were dealing with these amendments in the committee I suggested that it should be possible for veterans to pool their grants for the purpose of buying equipment. The director stated that he had a proposal under which veterans settling on provincial lands would be able to pool their grants, but I think we should go farther than that and make it possible for a number of veterans settling on privately owned land to pool their grants for this purpose. Then a subcommittee was appointed to consider the advisability of making the Veterans Land Act

Veterans Land Act

apply to cooperative farms, and that subcommittee brought in a report urging the government to investigate the question and see whether it would not be possible in future to make the Veterans Land Act apply to some form of cooperative institution. If both these things are done I believe they will help take care of many boys who otherwise will be deprived of the benefits of this act, and who may just have to take jobs. So that I urge the government to follow up these matters and see that provision is made for the pooling of grants to boys who want to settle on privately owned land, and also for the making of grants to those who want to enter upon some type of cooperative farming.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext:
I wonder if we could have some statement from the minister as to how farms for veterans are purchased. I understand that there are regional officers and a supervisor for each office; but who actually purchases the land; and is an analysis made of the soil to determine whether or not the property is suitable for farming purposes? I ask this question because I have had several complaints along this line, one in particular concerning a farm which was purchased for a veteran, in connection with which it was stated that a junior farmer had worked the land for about four years and finally had to give it up owing to the poor quality of the soil. In spite of that fact it was purchased, at quite a price, to be sold to veterans under the Veterans' Land Act. I was wondering how this land was purchased, and if an analysis were made of the soil to indicate its suitability for farming. That can be answered later on by the minister.
Then it seems to take considerable time to have these transactions put through. A veteran may decide to purchase a farm for post-war occupation, and will begin proceedings for that purpose. But six or eight months will have elapsed before the papers are finally completed, and he finds he must wait all that time to get on the land.
Then there is the matter of small holdings. Several small holdings have been opened up across the country, but for some reason or another there does not seem to have been any great effort put forth to have them completed. Is it because the prices are so high the veterans do not want to purchase them? The figures indicate that 3,000 of these small holdings have been started, but only about 400 have been completed1 to the present time. In my own district they seem to be held up for some reason or another. Is it because the

veteran feels he cannot afford to purchase at the prices asked? I should like to have the minister answer these questions.

Mr. Speaker, I thought the minister was going to reply, but since it appears that he is not at this time, I shall just add a few words to what the hon. members for Melfort (Mr. Wright) and Acadia (Mr. Quelch) have said.
I was on the subcommittee which discussed the possibility of cooperative farms being established under the Veterans' Land Act. It was evident in that committee, as it has been made evident by other discussions in the house, that many members of the committee had not the foggiest notion of what a cooperative is. I was surprised to hear them express fear that the venture would not succeed. I could understand people who never had occasion to face danger or risk expressing fear that something would or would not happen. But it was surprising to me to hear veterans of both wars express fear, particularly in view of the fact that everything had been promised by the veterans themselves, to remove that cause of fear.
In the first place, the illustration of Matador, which was used, indicated that the government of Saskatchewan was prepared to give financial support to the point where operations under the Veterans' Land Act would not lose money. They were not prepared to allow a veteran to settle in this way on crown lands unless the veteran expressed the desire to do so. Consequently, there was no possibility, so far as human foresight could be exercised, of any slip-up.
No one wants to make a mistake, no matter what it is. But even though it was explained to the committee that these men were given every opportunity to see all the pitfalls as well as the advantages, and were given the necessary assistance and support, the committee did not see fit to recommend that this be undertaken.
Because of that I am convinced there will be a good many veterans from Saskatchewan who would have liked to re-settle in that province, but who are not going to be able to get the land, even with the useful improvement set out in section 2 of the bill. I dhould like hon. members to understand the importance of giving that opportunity to these boys. It does not mean that every veteran will accept the opportunity; but it does mean

Veterans Land Act
that a section-perhaps a small section-of Saskatchewan veterans will want to do so, and, if they do, they should not be prevented by some regulation which someone is afraid to change.
We talk about venture capital and private enterprise, and there is more talk about those things from other sections of the house than from this one. But there is no more private enterprise in the world than that found in a cooperative. No one goes into it unless he is privately convinced that he wishes to do so. It is purely and strictly a private procedure, just as private as any enterprise can be in this world.
These men were promised certain grants under the Veterans' Land Act, because of their service. To prevent their getting them is not fair. Mr. Chairman, I have here the act itself, chapter 33 of 1942, and by virtue of that act which is to be amended by the bill before us only those can enjoy the benefits of the act who enlisted and went overseas, even though for just a Cook's tour, and those who have served in Canada for a period of twelve months. If any soldier for any reason whatsoever has not been sent overseas or has not served twelve months in Canada he cannot take advantage of the act. I find that that construction is wrong because the purpose of the act is twofold. It is designed to help the veteran who has had some farming experience and has a natural disposition to establish himself on a farm, but it has also the higher purpose of serving the country at large by establishing more good men on the land. Those reasons can be taken together or considered separately. If you take them together I do not see why, we should give better treatment to the man who has signed a paper for overseas service than we give to the soldier who has not signed such a paper but has abided by the law. Even if that man has not abided by the law he is entitled to enjoy all the benefits of the act for the superior reason that farmers are essential to this country, not amateur farmers but real farmers who can do well by working on the farm. In a moment I shall move an amendment to that effect.
The famine which some members of parliament predicted at the time we were fighting for the farmer is now showing itself. It is not only on the horizon; but even now in this country which has been so generously endowed by the Almighty, we are finding that the land does not produce enough to satisfy the requirements of the Canadian people. Therefore it is not simply a question of rewarding the veteran who was sent overseas; it is a question of public necessity. How many

times have I seen boys with a good agricultural background come into my office desiring to establish themselves on the land, on a farm of their own, perhaps because the old homestead that belonged to their father was not large enough to establish all his sons. lation will be those who enlisted and served for any length of time overseas and those who, having enlisted have served for twelye months in the forces in Canada or in some auxiliary service. This bill will be no improvement unless those who have had experience in farming and are real farmers have an opportunity to take advantage of the act and cultivate the soil. That is my point.
In order to enlighten the committee on the real purpose of this amendment and the motive behind it, I must recall the errors of the past, when people who were steeped in prejudice gave no chance at all to those who were entitled to the dignity of man. I have the highest regard for the farmers. It was taught to me in my family. I live in a semi-rural district. In my family I have been told since I was a little boy that the farmer is the feeder of the country, the man without whom we could' not eat at all, we would die of hunger. Therefore the case I argue now is not only the case of the veteran; it is the case chiefly of the veteran who is a farmer and who was put in the army in spite of the fact that his duty, his national duty, was to stay on the farm at the time. I regret that able young men who were on the farms were compelled to go into the army, and their case was not considered fairly at the time. It was not considered with justice and fairness, because the farmer was regarded merely as a slacker. I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, and I will maintain all the time I have an opportunity to speak, that the farmer who did not enlist during the war, the farmer who claimed exemption because his duty was to be at home, was not a slacker. I regret to say, from my personal knowledge, that a farmer who has reached the age of fifty is not in a position to do all the hard work on the soil. He must rely on the assistance of his young and robust sons to do ploughing, to clean ditches and perform other hard work. The old man suffers, perhaps, from reheuma-tism, at his age he can do only light work on the farm. I wonder whether the circumstances are similar in the west, where agriculture is mostly mechanized. What I have said is true of my district as well as of Ontario and the maritimes, and perhaps also of British Columbia. The farmer needs his young sons. I shall certainly be in order to read the preamble, because the preamble precedes clause 1, and besides that it is an illustration of the real purpose of the act. Let us see what it is:
Whereas many men now serving in the active forces of Canada have recorded their desire to settle on land or engage in farming when hostilities cease . . .
"Many men"! It is not true. It is not true because the boys who have left the country to go to the army have been uprooted. Very often when they live in the cities afterwards they do not want to return to the country because the work on the farm is very hard, painstaking. When they live in town and have facilities which ought to be available in the country, these boys are reluctant to go back to the the old homestead; they want to lead an easier life. That is my experience, after dealing with quite a large number of farmers. Therefore, when we find a few who are ready to go back to the farm they must be awarded the greatest advantages possible, precisely because of their intention to return to the painstaking and arduous work which is the lot of the farmer in this country, work which starts at dawn and finishes a long time after dusk. It is not true that many men are ready to go back to the farm after serving in the army. I am sorry to say that this is one of the bills of which the least advantage will be taken, for the very reason I have given, and it is precisely because I want the bill to be just as serviceable as possible to those who want to farm that I speak as I do now.
To continue with the preamble:
. . . and it is desirable that suitably qualified veterans be encouraged to seek rehabilitation in the agricultural industry.
Suitably qualified veterans! Who are the most suitably qualified veterans? It is those who had their training on the land. You cannot make a farmer by inviting a white-collar man to go to the farm and start doing business there. He will be a complete failure.

You must go to men of experience. Farming is an art, and very few men can excel in an art without having some experience of it. "Fabricando fit faber." And the most suitable of all are precisely those who are kept in clink now, more than a year after the war is over, just to satisfy the antiCanadian and anti-national animus of the brass hats who would lose their jobs if the clinks were closed. The committee will recall that the question was raised earlier this session as to the procedure being followed in giving veterans title to homes being built under the small holding scheme under the Veterans' Land Act. There were actual cases in which veterans who had been allotted houses and had made their arrangements to take possession and had given up other tenancies were told, when they came to take possession the homes allotted to them that, owing to the fact that the cost was more than S6.000, they would have to undertake to pay all the excess over $6,000 before they would be granted possession. That matter first came to my attention as a result of two cases which existed in Sherbrooke and which were personally investigated and can be verified. It is known that the same situation prevails throughout other parts of the country where building projects of thirty or forty houses in a group have been proceeded with under the small holdings scheme on a cost-plus basis, and I think the government passed a vote of a million dollars to equalize costs across the dominion.
When the director of the Veterans' Land Act was before the committee he admitted that in most cases the houses cost more than $6,000. So this recommendation was drafted and put to the committee suggesting that inasmuch as the government is prepared to subsidize the cost of a home up to $6,000 to the extent of 23J per cent of its value, they should make the same subsidy available with respect also to that portion of the cost over $6,000. The objection raised to that was that the veteran who was getting a $7,000 home would be able to get it for the same price as the veteran who was getting a $6,000 home. But the objection does not apply because, if you make the same proportion of subsidy available, it means that the same proportion of the total cost would be underwritten by the government. Many veterans have already made their plans and are prepared to take up these homes, and if an amendment is not passed embodying the recommendation of the committee they will either be unable to take up the homes or be unable probably to meet the payments imposed on them to get possession.
I submit that the increase in cost which has resulted in the homes costing more than was expected by the veteran is not the

The Minister of Veterans Affairs has repeatedly stated that he is not interested in housing as such. I maintain that the minister and every other hon. member and every citizen of this country should take an interest in housing as such, and particularly with reference to veterans, because it was the veterans' families who were unable to shuttle into houses as they became vacant during the period of the war. Now that they are trying to reestablish their families, as far as the veterans are concerned the war is not yet over. The minister should reconsider the building programme which has been undertaken under the small holdings legislation of the land act, and he should extend the terms under which veterans can take small properties. I do not wish to speak at great length, but I submit that it is our duty as members of the House of 'Commons to provide buildings for more than a favoured few who will be able to take the homes that have been built by the Department of Veterans Affairs. When we consider that less than two per cent of the veterans of Canada are at present enjoying the generous benefits of this act; when we consider that the rest of them have not had an opportunity to set up housekeeping on their own behalf in homes at the reasonable prices that obtained before the war; when we think of the gratuities which they have received, which, in terms of money may sound excellent but in terms of rent at $50, $60, $70 or $80 a month for very much limited accommodation is another matter, then I maintain that we have not done our duty adequately as citizens of Canada. Under these circumstances, when we speak of gratitude to those who served us in time of need, it is simply so much eyewash. There are things in the Veterans' Land Act to which I personally take exception. I went into it fully in the veterans committee, and I do not propose at this time to reiterate the arguments that I used there. But I am concerned about the series of regulations which have grown up as a result of the

Veterans Land Act
bringing together of the various housing schemes in Canada which include the small holdings under the Veterans' Land Act and the other housing schemes administered by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. I take some exception to the expressed opinion that the small holdings part of the Veterans' Land Act was primarily conceived as rural settlement on small holdings. I do not deny the fact that when the act was conceived in 1942 that was the basic idea; but I suggest that, as a result of conditions which were no one's fault and over which there was perhaps no possible control, the practice in the first two years has been to make it practically an adjunct to urban housing of veterans. That situation has arisen. The minister and others have said in the committe and here that, if recent methods continue there will be discrimination between veterans, the one within the city limits and the one oni the outside. I am aware that tlhere may be, but I suggest to the committee that that discrimination already exists, and I fear it will exist in greater degree if we depart sharply from the practice of offering the advantages of suburban homes to urban workers. If we stop that practice which has existed we shall have discrimination, which, to my mind, is equally bad as the discrimination within cities which the minister fears.
In the committee the director first informed us that the cooperation with reconstruction did not involve any amendment of the act or changes in the regulations. But already by agreement it has come about that the practice of extending small holding advantages to veterans who work in the cities has been curtailed by limiting the construction of houses in groups of more than six. With that I take no serious issue, because I am one of those who have always believed that it was not good practice from the point of view of rehabilitation to construct what I and others have sometimes called "veterans villages".
I conceive the proper measure of the rehabilitation of a veteran to be to permit him to come back to communal life in his community with as little to remind him of his military experience as possible and to set him apart from his neighbour as little as may be humanly possible. To me that is complete rehabilitation. I would remind the committee, the minister and all who have had anything to do with this matter, that the veterans department itself, in its literature, the government and most of us as candidates and members during the last two years have held out this idea to the veteran-I am speaking now of the veterans from the cities-that while it was not practicable or desirable for him to
go out into the country and become a full-fledged farmer-in many instances he is not capable of doing that, and in practically no instance does he want to do it-we had something for him. It was this: if he had a modest, steady income and if he was prepared to go outside the corporate limits of the city where he was employed and could meet the other qualifications he would be assisted to establish himself in a home on a better standard than he could maintain as a city dweller, at a lower cost, through lower taxation and various other considerations. We reduced the acreage to half an acre in some of these places. It is all right to say that we did that because there was a desperate need, we had to get the houses close together, and had to get contractors who would deal with these housing blocks, and so forth. All these things are true. I think the reduction to half an acre was a recognition that we had made a commitment to these city veterans. We were not able to go, and I do not think we should go, inside the corporate limits of a city of any size, and have veterans houses compete on the same street with war-time houses which are being built for veterans. I do not think we should do that.
Many of these city veterans delayed making their applications for veterans housing on the advice of members of the house and of the committee, and of people like myself. I have done it. I have said, "You have some time to decide; do not jump at it now. Wait until the pressure is off." That man may now find himself in a position, as a result of these agreements, where he cannot get into the scheme, and therefore, in these circumstances, he may not be able to get a house at all.
I have been told-and I accept it-that by this agreement the Department of Reconstruction and Supply are prepared to consider suitable applications of individuals and even of groups of six, even though the property selected falls within an adjacent municipality with a population in excess of 5.000; that is, if there is suitable land available. I am not very happy about that regulation because' I have had some experience and I know the intent behind it. I know what has been done. There are areas in the city from which I come where the municipalities of five, six or seven thousand immediately adjacent to the city limits still have vast open areas. If you insisted on a man going outside that municipality he would be twelve or fifteen miles out. I suggest that this is a situation which requires to be closely watched by the minister and by the administration. I realize it is not a direct reflection on this act, or on the
Veterans Land Act

administrator, except in so far as it is a matter of agreement with the Minister of Munitions and Supply and his officers.
If the result of this legislation is to make it difficult or impossible for a veteran who works in the city, and who normally lived in the city and who has the other qualifications for a home under the Small Holdings Act, to obtain that home, then I say the agreement will constitute a breach of faith with the veteran. I base that suggestion on the literature of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I base it on the information which has been given by the counsellors to veterans returning from overseas to every district of Canada. I base it on information and advice which I as a member and an employee of the Department of National Defence myself gave when I was in the service. I am concerned that this shall not be the case. I am not urging that we should compete within the city limits with wartime housing or any other housing scheme. Under the Veterans' Land Act I understand it is not practicable to house all the veterans of Canada on small holdings on the fringes of cities. I know that perfectly well, but I am concerned that it shall not happen that a veteran, if he works in a city and is going to get a small holding will only get it in the slums or in the bush, where his house will not be conspicuously better than some other chap has had, because that other veteran insisted on getting an urban house and took a wartime housing one.
What I have been saying is not a criticism; it is a warning, an indication of a danger, of something I think perhaps may indicate a trend. It is a frank warning that if what I fear develops, in my opinion it will be a breach of faith, and as such I shall raise as much ructions as I am capable of raising here and hereafter.

Veterans Land Act

additional l',600 applications which he said had been approved, but in which construction had not been commenced, that leaves 66 per cent of the applicants in connection with whom no start has been made to have them settled. I point out these figures again as indicating the strongest possible reasons why the minister should pursue this matter with all diligence in order to find some solution.
I should like to say something further, so as to dear up any possible misconception which might result from what the parliamentary assistant has said. He pointed out that veterans under the small holdings scheme were getting more generous treatment than veterans under any other housing scheme could get. The point that is relevant there is that the type of small holding I had reference to was not any small holding project under the act. The type I referred to were those eases where the government was in charge of the building. It made the contracts in most cases on a cost-plus basis, nevertheless it 'had control over costs; and for various reasons, perhaps beyond the government's control, costs increased.. But it was a government housing scheme. Therefore the veteran is in no way responsible for that increase in cost. My idea of it at first was that it would be for pensioners, in order to give them a little extra land, and something extra to do. It has now become a housing project.
My suggestion, however, was in connection with the administration of the act. I believe there is a bottleneck in many of the districts in connection with the searching of titles and the preparation of different documents. My information is that in certain sections there are one or two lawyers who are trying to do all the work, instead of spreading it over, and giving it to a greater number of lawyers in the smaller districts. For example, just before the dinner recess one hon. member referred to fifty houses in the township of Stearboro, and 100 in the county of Ontario. This effort has been made, by agreement with the Department of Reconstruction, and it is
expected that they will all be completed by the middle of September. I can tell my hon. friend that there are probably twenty applications for every house available under the scheme.

I am sure the committee has listened with interest to the discussion of these matters during the last hour or so. Arising out of that discussion, particularly the comments made by the parliamentary assistant and by the Minister of Veterans Affairs, I have two or three questions to ask.
The measure before us is one providing for certain amendments to the Veterans' Land Act. The primary purpose of the act was the reestablishment of veterans on farms. But a supplementary section provided for the building of homes on small holdings in the neighbourhood of urban centres. The parliamentary assistant has given some statistics with respect to that and the Minister of Veterans Affairs made one comment, about which I should like to ask him. He pointed out that the homes being built on these small holdings under the Veterans' Land Act are provided to those taking them, under more favourable terms than are the houses which are built under some of the other government schemes, and he intimated that the continuance of this programme would mean further discrimination with respect to the assistance rendered to veterans settling
Veterans Land Act

in urban centres and on these small holdings. The question I would ask him is this: How did the government come to get into that position and to bring in one measure which is more favourable to home builders than the others? I presume he has an answer.
The other questions I wish, to ask are prompted by the statistics given by the parliamentary assistant. He told us of the number of applicants for farms, the number of applicants for homes on these small holdings, the number of applications that had been approved and the number of veterans who have been settled under both schemes. I gathered from his remarks that the government was discontinuing the policy of making homes available to veterans under this small holdings plan because of what the minister called discrimination. If that is true, since the parliamentary assistant indicated that there were some 19,000 applications and some 4,700 or 4,800 veterans had been settled in homes, I would ask, at what point is the government discontinuing that project?
I have another question. The understanding was that these homes would not cost more than 86,000. The veterans who were assisted in purchasing them understood that they were to cost $6,000 or less, but in actual practice the government finds that many of the houses constructed are costing more than that. How many of these houses will cost $6,000 or less? How many of them will cost $6,000 or more? What is the estimated excess cost of all these houses above the $6,000 originally estimated? I hope I have made my questions clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA

I will answer my hon. friend's question in regard to the Veterans' Land Act and leave some of them to my assistant to answer. Before my hon. friend joined us in our councils here, we had formed a committee which worked hard for eighteen months. On that committee were many practical farmers, some of whom I think my hon. friend knows from Manitoba. After eighteen months' study that committee made some very fine recommendations, the basic feature of which was settlement on farms. At that time, as my hon. friend knows, prices for land were much less than they are to-day. The basic selling price then was $4,800, but we found it necessary about a year afterwards to raise that to $6,000.
Another recommendation which that committee made, which was entirely ancillary, was for small holdings, which was never considered to be a basic feature of the act, but as we went along we found it to be the most popular feature.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE AUTHORITY FOR SALES OF LAND, BUILDING MATERIALS, ET CETERA
speechtext: It is coming along and, I hope, will be successful. That was done because the other housing features were not then developed, except Wartime Housing Limited. But now we have the three features, Wartime Housing, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and the Veterans' Land Act housing all incorporated in one housing scheme. I have read the survey that was made of the soldiers overseas for the purpose of ascertaining what they desired to do on returning to Canada, and I am not surprised at the attitude of many of them. I have seen some of the results of the operation of land settlement after the last war; and I do not think this amendment, repealing section 3 of the act of 1942 and appointing a large staff consisting of a director and others, will meet the requirements. I do not believe that you will get many soldiers to sign agreements under these provisions. Many of the returned soldiers would like to take up market gardening on the outskirts of cities like Toronto and Hamilton, but too many restrictions are imposed upon them. I appreciate the principle of the bill, but I suggest that the minister and the Department of Veterans Affairs should be given the power to deal with these men. Many of the men want to take their gratuities and go in for market gardening. For the purpose they would like to buy a truck or a jeep, but they cannot do so and yet the very things that these men require are being thrown on the scrap heap. When the veterans want jeeps or trucks they are told to go to a dealer and see someone in Montreal in control of real estate. I have been communicating with one of those gentlemen for some time, as to soldiers getting into their homes, but I find that he is on holidays. When the veteran has to go to a dealer to buy a plough or a truck or a jeep he is charged three or four times more. Is it any wonder that these men are not going on the land?
The principle of settling men on the land started after the Fenian raid and1 it was again carried out after the South-African war. For a radius of sixty miles around our city veterans of the last war went in for dairy farming; they went into the live stock industry; they took up market gardening; and a system of roads, electrical railways, suburban railways, buses and so on was built up. One would naturally expect that with the return of these men's sons from overseas a great many of them would want to engage in these occupations, but I doubt whether you will get anyone to carry out the laborious provisions of section 2 of the new bill. The men are tied down to too many conditions. It would have been better for the act to leave the making of rules and regulations to the minister, instead of their being set out in the act. I do not believe that any soldier would care to sign the contract. The men were complaining. The minister has' attempted to make rules and regulations from time to time. If the rules and regulations were improved they would be better than sections 2, 3 and 4.

It would be helpful if the Minister of Veterans Affairs would make a statement as to the present policy with regard to establishing veterans on small holdings. This evening he gave us the history of what has happened. Either he or his parliamentary assistant has intimated that a change of policy was made within the last few weeks. In the course of a speech on housing on July 22, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply explained his idea of the small holdings policy. I should like to have confirmation of that policy from the minister to-night. Apparently the two departments are concerned. There must be approval by both the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. The remarks of the latter will be found at pages 36S1 and 3682 of Hansard. I understood him to say that from now on small holdings will be established
Veterans Land Act

only within the boundaries of centres of 5,000 people or less, with this restriction, that if such centre is on the fringe of a metropolitan centre of 15,000, then there would be no small holdings even in that town of under 5,000. He did say that there were certain exceptions; that where there was a city of more than 5,000 isolated in an agricultural area they might establish small holdings in that city. There were also certain other exceptions with regard to the fringe areas of a metropolitan centre. But he also said this-this is where some confusion comes into the picture.
We are very anxious to see the small holdings provision implemented to the full, provided it is implemented in the manner contemplated by parliament when the legislation was passed. My colleague and I have arrested a trend towards the small holdings section becoming a vehicle for financing veterans' urban housing.
I take it that means that if a veteran has two or three acres, no matter where it may be, he can come under the small holdings provision because originally that was the intention of the act. But in the veterans affairs committee Mr. Murchison told us the other day-unfortunately the proceedings of that day are not yet printed-that there is an arbitrary and definite prohibition established by the two departments against any small holdings going into certain centres. I questioned him about Greater Vancouver which the minister knows well, because we are both from that city, and Mr. Murchison said that there would be no small holdings established in the municipality of Burnaby, no matter whether the man had acreage or not. He said the same thing about North Vancouver and West Vancouver. The minister knows that in these municipalities there is land available for poultry ranches of two or three acres or for small fruits. It is ideal land for a small holding as we intended small holdings to be originally, and yet there is this arbitrary rule that there shall be no small holdings in these areas. I suppose there have been similar arbitrary rules made for other areas. That is contrary to the policy expressed by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. I would ask the Minister of Veterans Affairs to tell us now what the plan is at the present time.

I should like to say a word on this section. We have often heard it said that this act is primarily intended to assist veterans to establish or reestablish themselves in farming, to encourage them to farm or to resume their occupation if they were farming before going into the armed forces. In the areas of Canada suitable for farming, undoutedly this act will be of great assistance to veterans of that class. The director may acquire land and buildings, and may sell or agree to sell them to the veterans. He may even acquire land from the provinces or from the Minister of Mines and Resources; but representing Yukon here in this parliament I am chiefly concerned with the assistance required by veterans in that, part of Canada. We have veterans in Yukon with records as good as those of veterans in any other part of Canada; and their services in the war warrant them in asking and receiving assistance in reestablishment.
It is not practical to farm in Yukon on any extensive scale. They can produce farm products; they can keep dairy herds and so on. It is not a matter of the climate or the soil; it is the lack of any market. The market is too small to make farming worth while. Yukon depends entirely upon mining for its population. Successful mining means the success of that territory; unsuccessful mining means that the people move out. For the most part, the veterans in Yukon are miners returning to the mining territory to establish homes for themselves and their dependents. Those who are charged with the duty of administering this act seem to be doubtful whether under it assistance is possible for these veterans. First, in regard to the provision under which land may be acquired from the Minister of Mines and1 Resources, it has been established that the minister has no land in Yukon suitable to be taken up under this act; it has been all disposed of. I know the matter has received careful consideration by the minister and his staff. Apparently the physical and geographical conditions concerning Yukon have brought them to the opinion 
that this act cannot be applied to veterans there, but I think a careful reading of the let will show quite plainly that it is applicable and can be applied. How much broader could any statute be than the wording of section 7 of this act, which states:	'
The director may, for the purposes of this act,
(a)	purchase by agreement, at prices which to him shall seem reasonable, or
(b)	in any other manner acquire by consent or agreement from His Majesty in the right of Canada or from any province or municipal authority, or from any person, firm or corporation, such lands and buildings situate in any part of Canada and such other property including building materials, live stock, farm equipment and commercial fishing equipment as the director may deem necessary.
I am sure the officials administering the act, and also the minister, know that Yukon is part of Canada. Of course people who have not been west of Toronto do not realize that British Columbia, even, is in Canada. But here is this wide section 7 which refers to lands and buildings situate in any part of Canada. And they are purchased from whom? It is not from the province, not from the .territory, not from the Minister of Mines and Resources, but "from any person, firm or corporation". Any individual owning property there may sell it to the director, under the terms of section 7 of the act.
But to remove any doubt as to the application of the act to Yukon, and the settlements in Yukon, I wish to move an amendment, the effect of which will not be to broaden the scope of the act or to entail public expenditure beyond that now contemplated and authorized by the act, but which will apply explicitly to Yukon as part of Canada, and extend these benefits to Yukon veterans, giving them the assistance to which they are entitled.
I believe this is the appropriate time for this procedure, and I therefore move:
That there be added to section 35 the following:
"The director with the approval of the minister may acquire, convey, transfer, agree to acquire, convey, transfer land in Yukon territory including land within Dawson, Whitehorse and Mayo and subject to the provisions of this act and regulations made under this act may grant to veterans residing in Yukon amounts not exceeding the amount stated in subsection 3 of section 35 of this act, such grants to be used only for the purposes enumerated in subsection 4 of section 35 of this act."
I think that will set at rest any doubts which the administrators of the act, and perhaps the minister, may have.
